# PREFACE. <note>The original French heading "Avertissement" translates literally as "Warning" or "Notice," but in 18th-century publishing, it serves as the author's or editor's preface.</note>

Without the immense labors of M. de Sainte-Palaie <note>Jean-Baptiste de La Curne de Sainte-Palaye (1697–1781), a pioneering French scholar of medieval history and linguistics.</note>, the literary history of Europe, and of France in particular, would have always remained incomplete. Only the author of the *Memoirs on Ancient Chivalry* <note>Sainte-Palaye’s most famous work, which helped spark the 18th-century revival of interest in the Middle Ages.</note> could have snatched the troubadours from the tomb where their fame was buried along with their works. This respectable academician, sacrificing everything—health and fortune—to the deepest research into our national antiquities, has succeeded in discovering everything one could reasonably desire in a field of study bristling with thorns and capable of daunting even the most passionate thirst for knowledge. The Public will judge that this is not merely a discovery of idle curiosity, nor of fruitless erudition.

To know the troubadours, these ancient Provençal poets <note>While "Provençal" specifically refers to the region of Provence, it was historically used as a catch-all term for the Occitan language of Southern France used by the troubadours.</note>, the fathers of modern literature, it was necessary to find and explain their works. The King’s Library <note>original: "bibliothèque du Roi"; the royal collection that became the modern National Library of France (BnF).</note> possesses only four manuscripts of them. Italy possesses a great many. Although a love for antiquity and the arts had already led M. de Sainte-Palaie there, he undertook a second journey to collect so many unknown or neglected monuments... <note>The text ends mid-word with "négli-," the first part of "négligés" (neglected), continuing on the next page.</note>

<summary>This preface introduces the work of Jean-Baptiste de La Curne de Sainte-Palaye, creditng him with rediscovering the lost literature of the medieval troubadours through extensive archival research and travel to Italy.</summary>

Four years later, the learned Doctor Lami <note>Giovanni Lami (1697–1770), an influential Italian librarian and scholar.</note> celebrated them once again in an eloquent dedicatory epistle, where he likewise did justice to the qualities of his heart and those of his mind. (See *Delights of the Erudite* <note>original Latin: *Deliciæ eruditorum*, a multi-volume collection of historical documents published by Lami.</note>.)

If the French academician has exhausted, so to speak, all the libraries of Italy, this species of conquest required incredible activity, expense, and care. Let one judge this by a particular fact. The Fathers Mabillon and de Montfaucon <note>Jean Mabillon (1632–1707) and Bernard de Montfaucon (1655–1741) were giants of 17th-century scholarship; their inability to access these texts highlights the difficulty of Sainte-Palaie's task.</note> had been unable to obtain permission for certain manuscripts in Rome to be shared with them: M. de Sainte-Palaie, to obtain access to them, required a papal brief <note>A formal letter or decree from the Pope; here, it served as a high-level security clearance for restricted archives.</note>; whether a misguided literary jealousy or a self-interested policy had placed obstacles in the way of the progress of our knowledge.

After having collected about four thousand pieces, and the original lives of several poets; after having verified that the fragments scattered in various places, numbering twelve hundred, were all found in his collections; he still had the greatest difficulties to overcome. How was he to properly understand the troubadours? Men of Letters, though familiar with the Provençal tongue <note>The Occitan language of Southern France, which was the medium of the troubadours.</note>

Be that as it may, the merit of this work belongs especially to **Mr. de Sainte-Palaye** <note>Jean-Baptiste de La Curne de Sainte-Palaye (1697–1781) was a pioneering French scholar who dedicated his life to studying the Middle Ages, chivalry, and the Occitan language of the troubadours.</note>. I have only set to work with pleasure the materials that he gathered with so much effort. I have followed his translations, giving the style a freer and more varied turn. His remarks and those of his first collaborators have spared me the boredom of research. The selection and arrangement of the materials, the care in blending them together, of mixing in reflections, and of remedying as much as possible a tedious uniformity, do not require great efforts when one has such assistance. Although I have suppressed an infinite number of trivial things, I will perhaps be blamed for having left far too many. But what would be more than trivial elsewhere is not so in <term>literary history</term>, where **men of letters** <note>original: "gens de Lettres"; the intellectual elite and scholars of the Enlightenment era.</note> may find important what **people of the world** <note>original: "gens du monde"; refers to the fashionable, high-society audience who read for pleasure rather than rigorous study.</note> judge useless.

# PRELIMINARY
## DISCOURSE.

The <term>troubadours</term> <note>Lyrical poets and musicians of the Middle Ages who wrote in the Occitan language.</note> are now hardly known except by name; and most <term>men of letters</term> <note>original: "gens de Lettres"; a term for the educated elite or intellectuals of the period.</note> themselves form only a very imperfect idea of them. One is satisfied with knowing that these ancient <term>Provençal poets</term> <note>While the author uses "Provençal," modern scholars note they came from various regions in what is now Southern France where Occitan was spoken.</note> flourished as early as the twelfth century, when barbarism and ignorance still dominated Europe; that they visited the courts of princes and great lords, the only stages where their talents could shine; that they were favorably received there, especially by the ladies, to whom they dedicated their tributes and their <term>songs</term> <note>original: "chansons"; the primary medium of the troubadours, often focusing on themes of courtly love.</note>; finally,

martial <note>This continues the sentence from the previous page: "...others give themselves over to the fury martial."</note>: some act as the trumpets of **fanaticism**; others depict customs and rail against disorders; some even deal with philosophy. If **Nostradamus** <note>original: "Nostradamus"; referring here to Jean de Nostredame (1507–1577), the younger brother of the famous astrologer, who wrote a highly unreliable history of Provençal poets.</note> had only known a portion of the manuscripts of **Mr. de Sainte-Palaye** <note>Jean-Baptiste de La Curne de Sainte-Palaye (1697–1781), the scholar whose massive collection of medieval documents forms the basis of this work.</note>: however mediocre his talent for thinking and writing might have been, he would have left us at least an instructive and curious work.

I propose in this **Discourse**, not to highlight the importance of the subject, but to present it from a general point of view, which may allow its connections to be better understood. # PRELIMINARY REMARKS.

->b iij<-

...public events mixed with popular rumors and often ridiculous legends: they degraded history; they did not know it at all. But poets were naturally the painters of society. Among the ancients, Homer fills the gap in this regard for the lack of <term>historical monuments</term> <note>In this context, "monuments" refers to primary records, chronicles, or physical evidence that serves as a testimony to history.</note>, and even his fictions are a source of truths that could not be found elsewhere. Bembo <note>Pietro Bembo (1470–1547) was an influential Italian scholar and cardinal who argued that the Provençal language was the foundational model for Italian poetic style.</note> likewise asserts that this language possessed a great superiority over all those of the West, and that every man who wished to write well, especially in verse, wrote in Provençal. (*Prose, Book 1* <note>original: "Prof. 1."; this refers to Bembo's *Prose della volgar lingua*.</note>) A compilation of authorities would cost me only the trouble of transcribing the passages already cited by Bastero in the preface of his *Crusca Provenzale* <note>Antonio Bastero’s *La Crusca Provenzale* (1724) was a pioneering study that sought to document the influence of Troubadour poetry on the development of Romance languages.</note>. Indeed, at the end of the thirteenth century, Dante <note>Dante Alighieri (c. 1265–1321), the preeminent Italian poet whose work, particularly the *Divine Comedy*, transitioned literature from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance.</note> gave the impulse of genius to the Italian language. Petrarch <note>Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), an Italian scholar and poet; although he lived much of his life in Avignon (in Provence), his refined Italian sonnets set a new standard for European lyric poetry.</note> appeared, inspired by love; and under the very skies of Provence, he made heard such melodious sounds and such elegant verses; in a word, he so eclipsed the troubadours that their name, their language, and their poetry almost entirely vanished from the eyes of Europe.

France already had its own poets, rivals of the Provençals who were their masters, and Thibaut, Count of Champagne <note>Thibaut IV (1201–1253), also known as Thibaut le Chansonnier, was a celebrated *trouvère* (the Northern French equivalent of a troubadour) and King of Navarre.</note>, had distinguished himself among them. The troubadours pulled Europe out of a fatal lethargy: they revived spirits that appeared dead; by amusing them, they made them think. Through paths enameled with rustic flowers, they set them on the road to reason, and even toward perfection itself; and such is the chain of human affairs that one can attribute the greatest effects to this first, almost unknown cause. Every revolution in the human mind deserves to be studied with attentive curiosity, and the principles of a revolution deserve it at least as much as its progress. In this regard, how much should the troubadours interest us?

### I.
## WILLIAM IX, Count of Poitou & Duke of Aquitaine.

The first troubadour of whom we have record is a prince: several other princes will provide us with interesting entries. <note>William IX (1071–1127) is widely considered the first of the troubadours, or lyric poets of the Occitan language, whose work has been preserved. He was a powerful nobleman and the grandfather of Eleanor of Aquitaine.</note> It would be but a modest honor for literature if their pieces lacked merit; for literary glory is tied to the quality of the works themselves, and not to that of the au— <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page; the word is likely "authors" (auteurs).</note>

—thors. But independently of the remarkable qualities found in the productions of these poets, the insights they offer to history are curious in proportion to the role they played in the world. Our primary objective is to depict men and their customs <term>mœurs: the social customs, morals, and character of a specific era</term>. In times of simplicity, character reveals itself without artifice, even at the heart of courts; and the spirit of that age hardly disguised its true nature.

**WILLIAM IX***, Count of Poitou, born in 1071, died in 1122, made himself famous among his contemporaries. To the advantages of birth and fortune, he joined those of physical appearance, courage, and talent. He is criticized for a licentiousness of conduct, which seems to imply the refinements of luxury—

Ultimately, it matters little to us whether a prince of the twelfth century was wise or debauched; but it is of great importance to the human mind to observe how much judgments vary regarding the same person, and especially how false praise is when its principle is prejudice or self-interest.

If a writer’s morals are usually depicted in his works, those of William do not create a bias in his favor: their obscenity suggests debauchery. We have nine pieces by him. The poet concludes this tale with an *envoi* <note>A short concluding stanza of a poem, common in troubadour verse, used to address a specific person or summarize the work.</note> to his jongleur <term>jongleur: a professional entertainer or minstrel in medieval France</term>, whom he instructs to present the piece to the two ladies, while asking them on his behalf to exterminate their cursed cat.

What likelihood is there that a prince had such an adventure while traveling? It is probably nothing more than a fable, of William’s own invention. Terence’s *The Eunuch* <note>original: "L'Eunuque de Térence"; a famous Latin comedy by the Roman playwright Terence involving a character in disguise.</note> might have suggested the idea to him. But we would regard it as a miracle if he had even known this poet. One would be better founded in believing that Palaprat, who prided himself in our own day for having changed Terence’s *Eunuch* into a mute for our theater, took advantage of the piece by the Count of Poitou, which was known in 1667 through a work by Hauteferre.

->### OF THE TROUBADOURS.<-

Two other pieces by William are more or less of the same genre. In one, he recalls his sexual conquests; he thanks God and *St. Julian* <note>St. Julian the Hospitaller was the patron saint of travelers; in the medieval tradition of courtly love, he was also frequently invoked by lovers seeking good "lodging" or success in their romantic pursuits.</note> for them. He recounts, in the most indecent manner, his victory over a woman of the common people. Such was the dangerous superstition of those times: Heaven was invoked for the success of libertine enterprises, and *St. Julian* was especially the patron to whom one had recourse. In the second piece, William seems to play the part of the mysterious man regarding his gallant adventures: he does not name the heroines, but modesty is no less offended by the imagery.

The first of these pieces makes express mention of *jeux-partis* <note>A "divided game"; a poetic debate where one poet proposes a dilemma and another chooses a side to defend.</note> or *tensons* <term>tenson: a genre of troubadour poem taking the form of a contest or debate between two poets</term>, and of the prize won by the victor. This was the name given to the questions that the troubadours debated to show off their talents. # ON THE TROUBADOURS. 11

Two other pieces by William <note>William IX (1071–1126), Duke of Aquitaine and Count of Poitou, is the earliest troubadour whose work has survived.</note> are of much the same character. In one, he recalls his amorous successes; he thanks God and St. Julian <note>St. Julian the Hospitaller was the patron saint of travelers. In the medieval tradition of "courtly love," he was often invoked to ensure "good lodging"—a common euphemism for finding a receptive lover or a successful sexual encounter.</note> for them: he recounts, in the most indecent manner, his victory over a common woman. Such was the dangerous superstition of those times: one invoked heaven for the success of libertine <note>In this context, "libertinage" refers to a lifestyle of seeking sensual pleasure without regard for social or religious moral codes.</note> pursuits, and St. Julian was the particular patron to whom people turned. In the second piece, William seems to play the mystery regarding his gallant adventures: he names no heroines, yet modesty is nonetheless wounded by the descriptions.

The first of these pieces makes explicit mention of *jeux-partis* <term>jeux-partis: literally "divided games," these were poetic debates where one poet proposed a dilemma about love and another had to defend one of the options.</term> or *tensons* <term>tensons: (from the Occitan "tenso") a style of poem involving a contest or debate between two troubadours, often concerning matters of love, philosophy, or ethics.</term>, and the prize carried off by the victor. These were the names for the questions that the troubadours debated to display their talents. When a prince or high noble held a plenary court <note>A "plenary court" (*cour plénière*) was a grand ceremonial assembly held by a sovereign or great lord on major feast days, involving banquets, entertainment, and the settling of legal or political matters.</note>, they would—

The metaphysics of love, the usual subject of these disputes, provided them with abundant material. Numerous assemblies excited the verve of our poets; and prizes were distributed to those judged most worthy. This custom likely led to the institution of the *courts of love* (*cours d’amour*), which proposed similar questions and became their judges. No troubadour has spoken of these "tribunals of gallantry," although their pieces are full of allusions to the customs of their time. Thus, the *jeux-partis* <term>jeux-partis: poetic debates where two parties argue over a dilemma of love</term> do not at all imply the existence of *courts of love* <note>Historians continue to debate whether these "Courts of Love" were formal institutions or merely a literary fiction and social game played by the aristocracy.</note>; and Cazeneuve <note>Pierre de Cazeneuve (1591–1652) was a French historian and linguist who wrote extensively on the origins of the French language and the laws of the "Floral Games."</note> appears to be mistaken in maintaining that they are much older than previously believed *.

Four other pieces by the Count of Poitou contain nothing but gallantry.

A lady he loves rejects his vows: he will love her forever. He swears by the head of St. Julian <note>St. Julian the Hospitaller was the patron saint of travelers and hospitality; such an oath was common in medieval literature to emphasize the speaker's earnestness.</note>, that he will die if he does not obtain a kiss from her; at the very least, her severity will force him to become a monk.

In the eighth piece, he is no longer this faithful lover: he is a man who holds strongly to no object; whom no event affects with lasting impressions; whose flighty humor admits only slight attachments. *The fairies*, he adds, *made him thus*. We know of no older testimony regarding fairies; and, undoubtedly, they caused little sensation, since the troubadours did not profit at all from the resources they could have provided to poetry.

The ninth piece is of a devout tone, entirely opposite to the character of William <note>William IX was notorious for his conflicts with the Church and his irreverent lifestyle, making this sudden shift to piety particularly notable to historians.</note>. ### II.
## BERNARD DE VENTADOUR.

The liveliness and delicacy of feeling, the beauty of imagery, the simplicity of style, and the ease of versification distinguish this poet to his advantage; even Petrarch <note>Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), the famous Italian scholar and poet, who deeply admired the Troubadour tradition.</note> made mention of him with praise *. His obscure birth did not prevent him from shining in the courts. Although the common people then amounted to almost nothing <note>A reference to the rigid feudal system where social mobility was nearly impossible for those not born into the nobility.</note>, poetic talents compensated for a lack of nobility in our southern provinces, where every other literary talent was, as elsewhere, buried and left without practice.

Bernard was born at the castle of Ventadour, in Limousin <note>A historical province in south-central France.</note>. His father was a servant in charge of the oven <note>Essentially a baker or stoker; this highlights Bernard's exceptionally humble beginnings compared to the high-born William IX discussed previously.</note>. In every age, vanity was one of the great motivations of human life. The princes and lords of that time prided themselves on a hospitality that was often more ostentatious than useful: they wanted to shine through profusion <note>The French "profusion" implies an intentional, staggering abundance designed to overwhelm guests with the host's wealth.</note>. Their subjects made it a point of honor to contribute to it: flattering distinctions could easily become a lure to draw great sacrifices from them.

with a talent suited to make him dear and commendable there, Bernard found a pitfall <note>original: "écueil"; literally a reef or obstacle. Admiration inspired him at first; another sentiment was not long in animating him. The progress of love unfolds in his verses. "I cannot," he said, "hide from myself the turmoil of my soul; but by feigning to sing and to laugh, I will at least know how to hide it from those who observe me."

He sang indeed, sometimes of the return of spring, which restores the greenery to the trees, the enamel of flowers <note>original: "l’émail des fleurs"; a classic medieval poetic metaphor comparing a meadow filled with colorful flowers to the bright, decorative enamel work popular in the Middle Ages.</note> to the meadows, and the harmony of its voice to the nightingale; at other times, he sang of the power of love, the sweetness and the dangers of an attachment, the infidelity or the indiscretion of men, and the inconstancy and whims of women.

->24<-

Vain efforts to disguise his passion! He felt that it was only a means of sustaining it, and that love alone dictated his verses. This is what made him say in various places:

> "Good songs all spring from the heart. But the heart—who can animate it, if not love? . . . The joy that love births <note>original: "l’enfante"; literally "gives birth to." This reflects the medieval idea that "Joy" (Joï) was a specific, transformative emotional state for the poet.</note> penetrates me and passes into my songs to embellish them. Why be surprised by the success they have in the world? He who loves more must also sing better."

Then rising up against false lovers, he seems to complain to providence <note>In this context, the natural order or divine will that governs human traits.</note> that it has not stamped them with a distinctive mark. A horn in the middle of the forehead—that is the sign by which he would wish for them to be distinguished. Remove the horn, which today seems ridiculous <note>The author is likely referring to the "cuckold’s horns" or medieval satirical imagery, which by the 18th century was seen as low-brow or farcical.</note>, and you find the thought of Euripides <note>A classic Greek playwright (c. 480–406 BC) known for his psychological depth.</note> so well rendered by Racine <note>Jean Racine (1639–1699), the master of French classical tragedy. The lines quoted here are from his play *Phèdre*.</note>:

> And should we not, by certain signs,
> Recognize the hearts of treacherous humans?

Respect and the fear of displeasing held his tongue captive for a long time. At last, he dared to speak; and he found in the Viscountess <note>Marguerite de Turenne, the wife of his patron, Viscount Ebles III of Ventadour.</note> nothing but contempt. From this sprang those complaints of a passionate lover, scattered throughout his songs:

> "I know love only through the anxieties that agitate me; but these anxieties are dear to me. No, I would not change my torments for all the goods that men desire. Love, if your pains hold such charms for me, what would I say of your pleasures! Ah! let me love always, even without being loved *."

In another piece:

> "While the years have regular variations, and one season always gives way to another, I languish constantly—"

He found one at the court of the Duchess of Normandy, **Eleanor of Guyenne** <note>Better known to English readers as Eleanor of Aquitaine (c. 1122–1204), one of the most powerful and influential figures of the Middle Ages.</note>, who, after her divorce from **Louis VII** <note>King of the Franks.</note>, had married in 1152 **Henry**, Duke of Normandy, later King of England, **Henry II** [1]*.

This princess, all too well known for her romantic dalliances <note>original: "galanteries" — referring to her reputation for courtly flirtations and amorous adventures.</note>, welcomed the <term>troubadour</term> <note>A composer and performer of Old Occitan lyric poetry.</note> with a kindness full of esteem and respect. What he called *the tyranny of rank* was little able to intimidate his heart.

->ON THE DUCHESS OF NORMANDY.<-

[1] The Provençal author of our manuscript biographies states that Bernard went to find the Duchess of Normandy <note>Eleanor of Aquitaine (c. 1122–1204), a famous patron of the arts who became Duchess of Normandy upon her marriage to Henry II.</note>, and that Henry, King of England, having married her, took her from Normandy to England. He should have said that Henry, who had married her while still Duke of Normandy, took her to England when he succeeded King Stephen <note>Stephen of Blois, who reigned as King of England until 1154.</note>. Nostradamus and his copyists have mistaken Richard <note>Likely referring to Richard the Lionheart, son of Henry II and Eleanor.</note> for Henry II when speaking of the Duchess of Normandy. The historian of Languedoc <note>Referring to the authors of the *Histoire Générale de Languedoc*, a definitive historical work of the era.</note>, otherwise so judicious and exact, has fallen into the same error; convinced that it concerned Alix of France <note>Alys of France (1160–c.1220), daughter of King Louis VII, who was famously involved in the dynastic disputes of the English crown.</note>, daughter of Louis VII,

### III.
## GARIN D'APCHIER.

The House of Apchier, which still exists and is one of the noblest of Gévaudan <note>Gévaudan was a former province in southern France, now primarily the department of Lozère.</note>, takes its name from the castle of Apchier, located in that province. It has produced several individuals named Garin. This particular Garin lived under Raymond V, Count of Toulouse <note>Raymond V (1134–1194) was a powerful lord and a significant patron of the troubadours.</note>. His noble birth distinguishes him among the troubadours more than his literary works.

Garin d'Apchier was, according to our manuscripts, *valiant and a good warrior, a good troubadour, and a good knight; he knew well how to court women <note>The original French "faire l'amour" in this historical context refers to the stylized practice of Courtly Love rather than its modern sexual meaning.</note> and to be gallant; and he pushed his generosity to the point of giving away everything he possessed.* Judging by this praise, he must have enjoyed great esteem in his time. We find, however, no specific details of his feats of chivalry, nor of his romantic adventures. As a poet, he hardly deserves to be celebrated.

He is credited with the invention of the *descord* <note>The *descort* (from the Old Occitan for "discord") was a poetic form intended to express emotional distress through intentional "discordance" in meter, rhyme, or language.</note>, a genre of composition about which little is known. A manuscript glossary in French and Latin, held in the Laurentian Library in Florence <note>original: "bibliothèque de Saint-Laurent"</note>, interprets this word as a certain diversity and variation in song. Beyond this, we know nothing more.

Only five of Garin's pieces have survived to the present day; all are addressed to Communal, his *jongleur* <note>A jongleur was a professional performer who sang and played instruments, often performing the compositions of noble troubadours like Garin.</note>, whom he mocks quite coarsely. This old jongleur had a mania for playing the gallant and the poet—two roles as little suited to his age as to his intellect. In a first piece, the troubadour reproaches him for singing his verses poorly—verses that earn him his bread—and adds that the Countess of Béziers-Burlats <note>Adelaide of Toulouse (c. 1158–1200), known as the Countess of Burlats, was a famous patroness of troubadours.</note> urges him to dismiss him.

Stung, no doubt, by a reply from the jongleur, he returns to the attack with even more bitterness.

## IV.

# PONS DE CAPDUEIL.

Pons de Capdueil, a wealthy baron in the diocese of Le Puy <note>original: "le Pui", referring to Le Puy-en-Velay in modern-day Auvergne, France</note>, is described by the historian of his life <note>This likely refers to the "Vida," a short prose biography written in Occitan in the 13th century</note> as combining all the advantages of a handsome figure with the courage of a fine knight <term>chevalier: a noble-born soldier or knight</term>, the eloquence of a polished speaker, the manners of a pleasant and gallant man, and the talent for composing verse, singing with grace, and playing instruments. The Provençal author's <note>original: "l'auteur provençal"</note> only criticism of him was that he was too thrifty <note>original: "économe"</note>; a claim that would be hard to believe, he says, when seeing how he entertained company and used his wealth to bring himself honor.

A romantic love <note>original: "amour romanesque"; here referring to the highly stylized and ritualized "courtly love" practiced by the nobility and poets of the era</note> always had its refinements: the more it was filled with fantastic ideas, the more it was subject to bizarre whims. After having long possessed the favor of Azalaïs, and having cultivated it through so many festivals with which she seemed delighted, Capdueil suspected that she only loved him for the sake of these entertainments he provided for her. A secret jealousy gnawed at him and made him unfair. Insensible to all the proofs of preference he received, he thought only of testing a heart where he wished to reign through pure love.

In effect, he retired to Provence and affected an attachment to the wife of Roscelin, Viscount of Marseille <margin>[2] Roscelin was a prominent figure in the nobility of Marseille during the late 12th century.</margin>. # LITERARY HISTORY

The troubadour employed a better means. He had recourse to three distinguished ladies, whose mediation and pleas finally allowed him to return to favor. He swore never to stray from the straight path of love: his fidelity was indeed beyond reproach. We have twenty songs by him that this passion inspired. The minor details of these are of little interest.

Death having taken Azalaïs from him, he celebrated her in a lament <note>original: "complainte"; a mournful song or lyric poem expressing grief, a common genre for troubadours mourning a lady or patron</note>, wherein he says that the angels are occupied with praising her in paradise. Sorrow penetrates his soul; he no longer feels the same desires: he no longer wishes to sing, and renounces love forever.

Deprived of the object of his tenderness, plunged into a profound sadness, Capdueil effectively became devout <note>original: "dévot"; here meaning he transitioned from the secular "religion" of courtly love to actual religious piety</note>. He gave himself over to religious sentiments, so well-suited to filling the void that the passions leave in the soul. It is well known that the misfortunes of love have often inspired a taste for the <term>cloister: a monastery or convent; it was common for medieval figures to retire to a religious house after a life of worldly pursuits or personal tragedy</term>.

...cloister. But a knight at that time found ways to demonstrate his devotion without leaving the secular world: it was the era of the <term>crusades: a series of military expeditions sanctioned by the Church to recover the Holy Land</term>.

Not content with simply "taking the cross" <note>original: "prendre la croix"; the formal vow to join a crusade, usually marked by attaching a cross to one's garments</note>, the troubadour became, in a sense, a zealous preacher for the holy war. He composed two poems for this purpose, in which we find several quite remarkable features.

He states that the <term>vicar of St. Peter: a title for the Pope, emphasizing his role as the earthly representative of the Apostle</term> has sent absolution through his cardinals and legates, by virtue of the power he received to unbind all the sins of the world. Consequently, he urges Christians to obey the exhortations for the crusade and to go punish the outrages that the Turks are committing against the holy places. Does this use of the title "vicar," rather than "successor of St. Peter," imply a theological concept different from our own, or merely an inaccuracy by the poet? This is a problem that would be difficult to resolve perfectly.

One will not at least suspect him, on his part, of any design to weaken respect for the authority of the Pope.

He assures that by taking the cross <note>original: "prenant la croix"; the formal vow to join a crusade, often involving a physical cloth cross sewn onto clothing</note>, sinners will wash away their crimes without being obliged to embrace the monastic state. He promises paradise to those who depart, and threatens those who remain with hell. He excepts only the sick and the elderly; and even they must give money to the crusaders.

How far, then, did the superstitious prejudices of this century go! To march against the Turks, or to become a monk: there, according to Capdueil <note>Pons de Capdueil (c. 1160–1220), a troubadour known for his transition from courtly love poetry to religious zeal</note>, is the only path of salvation for sinners! One must run to Asia, weapons in hand, to avoid hell and to win paradise! Only the sick and the elderly are exempt from an obligation that tends toward the misfortune of families and the ruin of kingdoms! They are even forced to buy this <term>dispensation: a formal exemption from a church requirement, often granted in exchange for a pious donation</term> with money! It is

They had rather significant disputes together, but without a declaration of war.

### V.

## RICHARD I, King of England.

It is astonishing to find among the troubadours <note>The troubadours were poet-musicians of the 11th to 13th centuries who composed and performed Old Occitan lyric poetry, famously celebrating courtly love and chivalry</note> a king of whom historians speak only as a fiery warrior and a greedy, debauched tyrant. His poetic role was, undoubtedly, of little brilliance. Superior talents in a sovereign would not escape history; mediocre talents easily do so when they are obscured by violent enterprises or acts of oppression. Although Charles IX in France wrote fairly good verses, he is hardly known as a poet; instead, the Saint Bartholomew’s Day massacre <note>A targeted group of assassinations followed by a wave of Catholic mob violence against the Huguenots (French Calvinist Protestants) in 1572</note> made him famous.

RICHARD, son and successor of Henry II, King of England, of the house of Anjou-Plantagenet, had been made count

As a magnificent patron of the troubadours, he attracted many of them to his side. By amusing himself with their compositions, he learned to imitate them. Richard was no sooner set free than he sought to signal his vengeance against Philip Augustus <note>Philip II of France, Richard's former ally who had conspired against him during his imprisonment</note>. Arms were taken up in 1195. Small, murderous expeditions, featuring no memorable events, followed one another in rapid succession; for lack of resources, the parties were soon forced to suspend them. A truce was reached, by which Richard abandoned the province of Auvergne to Philip in exchange for Quercy. Because these provinces had their own immediate lords, the kings only exchanged the **high domain** <term>High domain (French: "haut domaine"): The ultimate feudal authority or suzerainty over a territory, rather than direct ownership or occupation of the land</term>.

According to our Provençal historian, the **Dauphin of Auvergne** <note>Robert I, Count of Clermont, who was among the first to use the title 'Dauphin'</note> and **Count Guy**, his cousin, were very distressed to have as their suzerain an ambitious, harsh, and greedy monarch like the King of France. A fortress that Philip acquired in the province, and the rich town of **Issoire** which he seized, foreshadowed further troubles for them.

Such pieces will always be interesting, with their somewhat coarse simplicity. Although inferior to the speeches that Homer <note>The author compares the direct, warrior-like speech of the troubadours to the heroes of the *Iliad*</note> lends to his heroes, they nonetheless naturally depict the customs of an age comparable, in several points, to the heroic times of Greece. Moreover, the poet here is the very character of the action; this gives a quite particular value to this kind of monument <note>In this context, "monument" refers to a lasting historical record or literary work</note>.

This was likely the ordinary tone of quarrels between kings and lords. The feudal system <term>feudal system: a social and political hierarchy where land was held in exchange for service and loyalty</term> placed them, in a sense, on equal footing, because they lived in a state of continuous warfare. A lord's bravado against his own sovereign was not surprising then; it was even less surprising against a foreign king, especially when that lord had Philip Augustus <note>Philip II of France (r. 1180–1223), the first to call himself "King of France" rather than "King of the Franks"</note> as his own king and support.

The fiery Richard fell victim to a private dispute with a gentleman of Limousin, his vassal, whom he wanted to force to yield a treasure found on his land <note>Legend says a local lord found a hoard of gold statues; Richard, as his overlord, claimed it for himself, leading to the conflict</note>. In 1199, he was besieging the castle of Chalus <note>The Castle of Châlus-Chabrol in central France</note>. A shot from an arrow caused his death.

### VI.

## ARNAUD DE MARVEIL.

Although Petrarch <note>Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), the Italian scholar and poet who was a great admirer of the troubadours</note> calls this poet *the less famous Arnaud* <note>original Italian: "il men famoso Arnaldo"</note>, and places him below Arnaud Daniel <note>Arnaud Daniel (active late 12th century) was known for his "trobar clus" or "closed" style—complex and difficult poetry</note>, of whom we shall speak elsewhere; we do not fear to say that the former deserved a greater reputation than the latter. In truth, one finds in him the flaw of nearly all his contemporaries: a sometimes barren abundance, where ideas and sentiments are as if stifled by words. Several of his pieces consist of about two hundred lines, and one has four hundred, even though the subject matter required far fewer. But his versification is flowing, full of naturalness and tenderness; finally, between the two Arnauds, this one should have been the primary choice for Petrarch

the great master of love. (See **Arnaud Daniel** <note>Arnaud Daniel was a contemporary troubadour known for his complex style; the author here suggests Marveil's simpler, more emotional style is superior</note>.)

**Arnaud de Marveil** was born at the castle of that name in Périgord <note>A historical region in southwestern France, now roughly corresponding to the Dordogne department</note>. Since his parents were poor and of humble station, he sought to make his fortune through his talents. At first, he embraced the profession of *clerk*, or notary; for notaries shared the title of *clerk* <term>French: clerc; in the Middle Ages, this referred to any literate man capable of writing legal or religious documents, not just priests</term> with the clergy, and the name is still given today <note>Refers to the late 18th-century context of this manuscript</note> to the subordinates who work in their offices. He soon realized that, with a handsome appearance and a taste for poetry, he could play a more advantageous and pleasant role. Dissatisfied with his station, he presented himself to the world as a troubadour: this was the way to make a name for oneself among the great lords. The natural drive of his genius might have drawn him toward this path, but self-interest and ambition likely spurred him even further.

Every distinguished lord lived like a prince. One could count almost as many courts

This countess was Adelaide [1], daughter of Raymond V, Count of Toulouse, and wife of Roger II, nicknamed **Taillefer** <term>French: literally "Iron-cutter"; a common epithet for medieval warriors renowned for their strength in battle</term>, Viscount of Béziers. According to the custom of the age, women retained the title of the house from which they came when that of their husband was of a lower rank; as is still seen today in England and Germany. Hence this title of Countess, which the wife of a viscount bore.

To be well-received by princesses, to celebrate them out of gratitude, then to love them with passion, and to address to them the tenderest and yet the boldest vows all at once, seemed to be the destiny of a great number of troubadours, and the effect of the charm of the Provençal muses <note>The "muses" refers to the poetic inspiration and the specific Occitan language used by the poets of southern France</note>. The role of the **troubadours** <note>Medieval poet-musicians of Southern France who composed and performed lyric poetry, often centered on themes of courtly love.</note> resembled in some ways that of the knights. Both devoted themselves to the glory of their ladies; the latter as heroes, the former as **men of wit** <note>original: "beaux-esprits"—referring to those who display brilliance of mind and literary talent.</note>. Both sought to please, if only to satisfy a lady's vanity. These relationships would begin as a form of pure **gallantry**; but they often ended in dangerous intrigues.

Being able to approach **Adelaide** more freely, and receiving from her specific signs of kindness, Arnaud fell passionately in love, yet he could not capture her heart.

In a long introduction <note>original: *exorde*, the formal opening of a rhetorical or literary work</note> (for the merit of brevity <note>original: *précision*</note> was then little known), the author makes it a duty for learned men to share their enlightenment with others. He teaches the art of conducting oneself in the world: to make a just discernment between the good and the wicked; to distinguish the times and places suitable for either wisdom or folly; to know how to avenge oneself for insults and to recognize kind deeds; to apply blame and praise in an equitable manner—such are the rules he proposes after his pious opening. Knowledge <note>original: *la science* — in this medieval context, this refers to learning, wisdom, or the arts rather than the modern experimental sciences</note>, like a messenger, proclaims the glory of a man of merit. That of a knight <term>chevalier: a member of the medieval warrior class, expected to follow a code of chivalry and courtly behavior</term> is to fight well, to lead a troop well, to perform his service well, to be well-armed, to ride a horse well, to present himself with good grace in the courts, and to make himself agreeable there. > “...are the lot of ladies. Beauty is a great asset; however, it serves little without wisdom. The bourgeois <term>bourgeois: in this medieval context, residents of a town or city, typically merchants or craftsmen, who held a distinct legal status between the peasantry and the nobility</term> can acquire respect through integrity, through an obliging character, and through a foundation of politeness, gaiety, and frankness. If they have a pleasing appearance, if they speak well, they can find favor in the courts, play the part of the gallant, and be admitted to festivals. Among the clerics <term>clercs: educated men in religious orders who often served as administrators, scholars, or secretaries</term>, some possess knowledge, eloquence, and fine manners; others, goodness, integrity, and good conduct. Thus, in every station of life, one achieves respect, provided that one strives to deserve it through honorable sentiments.”

This maxim leads the poet to a tirade <note>original: *invective*</note> against the powerful of the age, who make themselves worthy of contempt by the abuse of their privileges. 

> “Established solely to keep the world at peace, to provide an example of clemency,”

## GEOFFROI RUDEL.

**GEOFFROI RUDEL**, according to the Provençal historian of his life <note>Referring to the *vidas*, the medieval biographical sketches that often blended fact with poetic legend</note>, was prince of Blaïa, that is to say, of Blaye, near Bordeaux. A singularly romantic love distinguishes him among the troubadours. What we are about to relate will no doubt seem like a romance; but the ages of chivalry produced adventures as true as they are improbable. ...and left five sons: Foulques, Geoffroi Rudel, Arnaud, Guillaume, and Adhémar. Geoffroi Rudel received the lordship of *Blaye* as his share. At first glance, he appears to be our troubadour. But how can we reconcile, through the dates, his passion for a Countess of *Tripoli*? This city was not captured and established as a county until around the year 1109. He had signed a charter in 1040, as reported by *Besly* (page 339). He would, therefore, have been too old after the conquest of *Tripoli* for us to attribute such a violent and romantic love to him. Furthermore, the founding of the *Templars* <note>The Knights Templar, a Catholic military order founded in 1118 to protect pilgrims in the Holy Land.</note> only dates back to the year 1118; and the troubadour was buried in their house. This is a new difficulty, which we consider insurmountable.

*Geoffroi Rudel* having died without heirs, the lordship of *Blaye* was reunited with the county of *Angoulême*. But it was subsequently broken up again, either as an inheritance for a younger son <note>The term used is "apanage," a provision made for younger children of a noble house who would not inherit the main title.</note>, or for some other reason. In the documents of the *Gallia Christiana* <note>original: "Gallia Christiana"; a monumental work in Latin documenting the history of the dioceses and abbeys of France.</note> (Vol. 2, p. 484), we find a *Gérard de Blaye*, father of a *Geoffroi Rudel*, who must be the same man whose signature appears at the bottom of a safe-conduct from the year 1231, in these terms: *G. Rudel, Lord of Blaye* <note>original: "G. Rudelli dominus de Blaya"</note> (ibid. p. 289). Could this be the troubadour? But if the Count of Tripoli is not enough

...too old for the first hypothesis, we fear that he did not survive long enough for the second.

Raymond II, the fourth count of Tripoli, having no children, gave his county to Raymond of Antioch, his cousin, and died in 1187. (*William of Tyre, Book 21, Chapter 5*) <note>original: "Guil. Tyr. l. 21. c. 5."; William of Tyre was a 12th-century prelate and the most important chronicler of the Crusades.</note> The latter similarly gave it, around the year 1200, to his brother Raymond IV, Prince of Antioch. Since that era, the county of Tripoli, joined with the principality of Antioch, has not had, it seems, any independent lord of its own. The adventure of *Geoffroi Rudel* cannot therefore be placed before 1118 nor after 1200. We have indicated in his biography the most likely way to reconcile it with history. The princess **Mélisende**, daughter of Raymond I <note>Mélisende of Tripoli, whose failed betrothal to the Byzantine Emperor became a major diplomatic scandal of the era.</note>, was betrothed to **Manuel**, Emperor of Constantinople, who later rejected her. This insult must have caused much talk about her and undoubtedly enhanced her reputation. The praise of the Pilgrims, whose favor she had perhaps won through her charity, was capable of firing the vivid imagination of the **troubadour** <note>A composer and performer of Old Occitan lyric poetry during the High Middle Ages, often focused on themes of courtly love.</note>. Finally, it is probable that this princess, rather than any wife of the counts of Tripoli, embraced a religious life <note>Meaning she entered a convent to become a nun.</note>. These are the foundations of a conjecture <note>An opinion or conclusion formed on the basis of incomplete information; an educated guess.</note>, which we do not present as a certain fact.

# V I I I.

## B E R N A R D - A R N A U D DE MONTCUC.

Our manuscripts contain no specific details regarding the life of this **troubadour** <term>A poet-musician of the 11th to 13th centuries who wrote in Old Occitan, the language of southern France.</term>; and the authors who have written on **Provençal poetry** have no knowledge of him. There are two castles named Montcuc, one in **Quercy**, the other in **Rouergue** <note>Historical provinces in the south of France.</note>. Bernard-Arnaud was apparently the lord or a native of one or the other.

A **sirventes** <term>A type of poem, often satirical or political, written by troubadours to the melody of an existing song.</term>, in which **satire** is singularly mingled with **gallantry**, is the only piece we have by him. One will see in it, as in several other historical monuments <note>original: "monumens"; here the author refers to surviving literary texts as "monuments" of history.</note>, the liberty taken by ancient poets to censure the conduct of princes. Perhaps nothing is more curious in their works. For

To understand this poem, we must indicate the historical fact to which it seems to relate.

Henry II, King of England, after his marriage to Eleanor, heiress of the Dukes of Aquitaine, renewed the ancient claims of these dukes to the County of Toulouse [1]. Resolved to assert them by force of arms, he besieged Toulouse in 1159. Louis the Young <note>King Louis VII of France (reigned 1137–1180), so named because he was crowned during his father's lifetime.</note> threw himself into the city and forced him to lift the siege. Count Raymond V recognized only the suzerainty <term>The right of a feudal lord to receive technical allegiance from a vassal without having direct control over their internal affairs.</term> of the Dukes of Aquitaine, saving the rights of the French crown. This expedition of the King of England provided material for satirical barbs. Let us listen to our poet.

### IX.

## PIERRE ROGIERS.

Pierre Rogiers was a gentleman of Auvergne. His parents destined him for the ecclesiastical state, and he became a canon <note>A member of the clergy who served in a cathedral.</note> of Clermont. But the strength of his inclination drew him elsewhere. Although he was *learned in letters*, according to the Provençal historian <note>A reference to the early biographers of the troubadours, who often wrote 'vidas' or life stories of the poets.</note> (a compliment that did not then imply great knowledge), he loved the world and its pleasures more than study and seclusion. Bored with his canonry, he became a <term>troubadour</term> <note>A lyric poet and composer of the High Middle Ages.</note> and even a <term>jongleur</term> <note>A professional entertainer who often performed the songs composed by troubadours.</note>. One can hardly resist the impulse of genius. Moreover, if one considers only fortune, the courts offered a bright prospect to poets.

Ermengarde, the eldest daughter of Aymeri II, Viscount of Narbonne—who was killed in 1134 at the Battle of Fraga in Spain against... <note>The sentence continues on the following page, likely referring to the Almoravid forces.</note>

OF THE TROUBADOURS. 109

Pierre Rogiers was, according to him <note>Referring to Jean de Nostredame (c. 1522–1577), the historian mentioned on the previous page whose work is being scrutinized for accuracy.</note>, at the court of Ermengarde of Narbonne, the wife of Roger Bernard, Count of Foix. He thus confuses Ermengarde, the daughter of Aimeri IV—who married the Count of Foix in 1232—with the Viscountess Ermengarde, her great-aunt <note>The Viscountess Ermengarde (r. 1134–1192) was the actual patron of the troubadours; Nostredame's confusion places the poet in the wrong century.</note>. He adds, on the authority of Hugues de Saint-Césaire, that Rogiers was in the city of Grasse in 1330, when the antipope Pierre de Corbiéri <note>Known to history as Nicholas V (r. 1328–1330), he was the last of the "Imperial" antipopes to be set up in opposition to the Popes at Avignon.</note> solemnly abdicated the tiara there. But this antipope did not abdicate at all: he was seized by the emissaries of John XXII, who caused him to die in prison.

It is evident that in historical matters, authorities must be subjected to critical examination. Nostradamus has been cited a hundred times as an oracle, because the Provençal poets were known almost exclusively through him; yet this oracle is constantly found to be in contradiction with the truth.

## X.

# AZALAÏS DE PORCAIRAGUES.

If chivalry <note>The medieval system of knighthood, characterized by a code of honor and the idealization of courtly love.</note> inspired heroines to contend with men for the glory of bravery, it is not surprising that Provençal poetry inspired women with the desire to distinguish themselves in the career of the troubadours <note>Known as *trobairitz*, these were female poets of the 12th and 13th centuries who composed and performed lyric poetry in the Occitan language.</note>. The vivacity of their imagination and the sensitivity of their souls led them there naturally. It is a matter of debate whether women are suited for great works of genius; but there is no doubt that they can excel in every genre of composition where sentiment and grace constitute the principal merit.

Azalaïs de Porcairagues is the first whom we find among our poets. According to our manuscript lives <note>original: "vies manuscrites." ### XI.

## PIERRE RAIMOND.

Pierre Raimond, according to the historical note in the collection of his poems, was the son of a citizen <note>original: *bourgeois*; at the time, this referred to a free inhabitant of a city who held certain legal rights and status, typically below the nobility but above the peasantry.</note> of Toulouse. His sharp and nimble mind, his wise character, and his talent for verse and song made him well-suited to succeed in the courts. Those of Alfonso (II), King of Aragon, Raymond (V), Count of Toulouse, and William (VIII), Lord of Montpellier, retained him in turn. He eventually married in Pamiers, where he died.

His history is entirely different in Nostradamus <note>Jean de Nostredame (c. 1522–1576), whose *Lives of the Most Celebrated Ancient Provençal Poets* is a famous mix of genuine history and fabricated legends.</note>. But, without dwelling on the minutiae of the subject, it is enough to observe that this strange historian records his death in 1225, yet also has him travel to Palestine in the retinue of the empe-

Seventeen gallant poems <note>original: *pièces galantes*; poems centered on courtly love and social refinement</note> by Raimond, though written in a tender and natural style, provide us with few remarkable features. The trivialities of love are so tedious to read! We shall take care to avoid them in our excerpts.

The poet is in love with a lady whom respect prevents him from naming. "She will be easily recognized," he says, "when I speak of her lovely smile, her beautiful eyes, her charming manners, her gaiety, and her pleasant conversation." After the lady rejected his vows, he abandoned his homeland and carried his sorrow to Aragon <note>a medieval kingdom in what is now northeastern Spain, known for its patronage of troubadours</note>. But love follows him, and the regrets of his absence devour him.

### XII.

## GUILLAUME DE BALAUN* & PIERRE DE BARJAC.

These two troubadours <note>Troubadours were lyric poets and performers of the 11th through 13th centuries, primarily from Southern France, who wrote in Occitan (the "langue d'oc").</note> cannot be separated. History presents them united in the same scene, where their loves and their verses are mutually intertwined. Based on the historical notes in our manuscripts, we shall report circumstances that would clearly seem fancifully invented <note>original: *imaginées à plaisir*; meaning stories created purely for entertainment rather than factual reporting</note>, were there not so many proofs of the eccentricities of that era.

GUILLAUME DE BALAUN, a noble—

(*History of Languedoc, vol. 2.*) A branch of this house could have been established in the lordship of Montpellier.

### X I I I.

## PIERRE DE LA MULA.

This unknown <term>troubadour</term><note>A lyric poet and musician, typically of noble birth, who composed in the Occitan language.</note> has left behind a curious <term>sirvente</term><note>A genre of medieval lyric poetry, usually satirical or political, used by poets to express grievances or social critiques.</note> in which he complains that an infinite number of men without talent are meddling in <term>jonglerie</term><note>The profession of the jongleur—a performer who traveled to courts to sing the songs of troubadours or perform entertainment.</note>. We see therein that this profession had become the resource of despicable people who joined insolence to baseness. "I wish to abandon," he writes, "the service of the jongleurs; for the more one serves them, the less one gains. They have multiplied to the point that there are as many of them as there are rabbits in a warren: we are flooded with them." The poet reproaches them in coarse terms for their habit of going two by two, crying *give to me*, for *I am a jongleur* <note>original: "donnez-moi, car je suis jongleur"</note>; and of insulting those who give them nothing. "I do not understand how such people can be admitted into the courts."

<sig>F v</sig>

<summary>This page introduces the troubadour Pierre de la Mula and describes his satirical poem (sirvente) criticizing the decline of the jongleur profession due to overcrowding and lack of talent. > ” I invite all courtly <term>jongleurs</term><note>Professional performers and entertainers of the Middle Ages who sang, played instruments, and recited poetry.</note> to
> ” rise up, like me, against this
> ” evil breed, with whom we
> ” should have nothing in common. “

The profession of jongleur, and even that of the <term>troubadour</term><note>A lyric poet-composer, often of noble birth, writing in the Occitan language.</note>, was bound to degenerate in this way. As soon as an attractive career is opened to talent, while it may excite the emulation of some, it tempts the starving greed of a much larger number. These individuals throw themselves into it, not with a noble desire to distinguish themselves, nor with the natural gifts necessary to succeed, but with a prevailing taste for profit and the baseness inspired by necessity and servile habits. Thus, for every one truly estimable man, a hundred vile charlatans infest society; and often their personal infamy reflects upon the very profession they dishonor.

Another <term>sirvente</term><note>A genre of satirical or political poetry used to express grievances or social critiques.</note> by Pierre de la Mula, directed against the avarice of the lords, offers nothing of note.

### XIV.
## ALFONSO II, King of Aragon.

A lengthy article could be written about this prince, if one wished to clarify the historical details concerning his house and the manner in which it ascended to the throne. However, one would only succeed in boring the reader with dry and misplaced erudition. Let us be content to say that Alfonso's father, Raymond Berenguer IV, Count of Barcelona, had married the heiress of Aragon; that the County of Provence, along with the viscounties of Carlat in Auvergne, Millau in Rouergue, and Gévaudan, had passed to his house through another marriage; and thus Provençal poetry <note>The lyric poetry of the Occitan language, which flourished in southern France and northern Spain during the High Middle Ages.</note>, which was making such progress, was bound to easily find its way into this court.

Alphonse died in 1196, after having strengthened his authority in Catalonia, Aragon, and Provence. Crescimbeni <note>Giovanni Mario Crescimbeni (1663–1728), an Italian literary historian who chronicled the history of vernacular poetry.</note> observes that he was not the only troubadour of his house. Zurita <note>Jerónimo Zurita (1512–1580), a renowned Spanish historian who wrote the definitive annals of the Kingdom of Aragon.</note>, cited by this writer, says under the reign of John I that the kings of Aragon, and particularly this one, placed great value on the art called <term>gai saber</term> <note>Literally "the gay science" or "joyful knowledge," a technical term used to describe the rules, craft, and philosophy of troubadour poetry.</note>, and that to encourage talent, they showered those who cultivated it with privileges. (*Annals of Aragon*) The name <term>gai saber</term> (gay science, or the science of joy) effectively designated Provençal poetry; but the same idea passed into other languages, and the poetry of that time, according to Zurita, was in Catalan. Moreover, John I could favor poets without being one himself. Peter III, king of Aragon, will have his own entry among our troubadours.

### XV.
## GUILLAUME DE CABESTAING.

I must frankly admit that the life of this troubadour <note>Guillem de Cabestany (c. 1162–1212) was a famous knight and poet from the Roussillon region. It is true that certain details, especially certain conversations, reveal a historian who embellishes his subject. But one can level this same criticism against several historians of antiquity; and besides, the naive traits found therein, though undoubtedly of the writer's invention—

By saying that he sings no vain praises, like other poets, Cabestaing assesses quite accurately the eulogies they always lavish, even upon imaginary mistresses. Was he not also exaggerating the perfections of his lady? A true lover might well be suspected of doing so. It is certain, at least, that Marguerite's reputation did not remain out of reach <note>original: "hors d'atteinte." This refers back to the closing lines of the previous page where the poet claimed her honor was safe from harm.</note> for long. Courtiers have such a keen eye for perceiving evil, and such a light tongue for revealing it! Cruel rumors reached Raymond <note>Raymond of Castel-Roussillon, the husband of Marguerite and the feudal lord to whom Cabestaing served as a knight and poet.</note>. He was all the more struck by them because he loved his wife and relied on the integrity <term>integrity: "honnêteté" here refers to the medieval code of conduct where a servant or vassal owed absolute loyalty and moral uprightness to their lord</term> of his servant.

Hunting with small hawks was a common pastime for the nobility and their courtiers.</note>. Cabestaing, being pressed for an answer and wishing to throw Raymond off the scent <note>original: "donner le change." They belonged to the Kings of Majorca, from the same house, when Alfonso IV, whose reign began in 1327, pursued James III—the last of these kings—for the crime of felony <term>felony: in a feudal context, a breach of the oath of loyalty between a vassal and their lord</term>, and stripped him of his states. # XVI.

## GAVAUDAN THE ELDER.

The pieces of this troubadour <note>troubadour: a lyric poet and musician of the 11th through 13th centuries, typically writing in Occitan</note>, of whom no writer makes mention, contain features worthy of curiosity. He flourished at the end of the twelfth century, since he mourns the loss of Jerusalem, which Saladin had conquered in 1187. The manner in which he exhorts Christians to fight the infidels is remarkable for the tone of simplicity and the insults inspired by the coarseness of manners <note>The author likely refers to the blunt, aggressive language common in medieval "sirventes" or political songs, which appeared "coarse" to readers of the 18th century.</note>.

### XVII.

# RAMBAUD D’ORANGE & THE COUNTESS OF DIE.

Two illustrious figures are the subject of this article; but their history offers few interesting details, and their compositions suggest little more than corrupt morals. <note>The author here adopts a moralizing tone common in 18th-century literary histories, often critical of the "courtly love" themes in troubadour lyrics.</note> Our manuscripts contain only a few pieces by Rambaud. The Historian of Languedoc <note>This likely refers to the Benedictine monks Dom Devic and Dom Vaissète, authors of the monumental *Histoire générale de Languedoc*.</note> will give us an idea of his person.

Rambaud was the son of Guillaume d’Omelas, of the House of Montpellier, and of Tiburge, the only daughter of Rambaud, Count of Orange, who died during an expedition to the Holy Land. <note>A reference to the Crusades.</note> Tiburge, by her will made in 1150, named as heirs her two sons Guillaume and Rambaud, who shared between them the...

One would not imagine that the ages of chivalric gallantry could have given birth to such a production. How can it be reconciled with the knights' religious respect for ladies? In the same way as the misconduct of so many Christians is reconciled with the sanctity of their belief. Contradictions between principles and morals are all too common, even in ages of reason <note>The author is likely referring to the Enlightenment era in which they are writing, comparing medieval inconsistencies to those of the 18th century.</note>.

Our manuscripts inform us that Raimbaut was loved by the Countess of Die <note>The Countess of Die (Beatriz de Dia) was one of the most famous *trobairitz*, or female troubadours, known for her poems about her love for Raimbaut d'Orange.</note>, who married William of Poitiers, the progenitor of the Counts of Valentinois and Diois, of the name Poitiers, whose last branch became extinct in our day.

Rambaud of Orange died around the year 1173 in Courthézon. Nostradamus <note>This refers to Jean de Nostredame, the younger brother of the famous astrologer; he wrote "The Lives of the Most Celebrated and Ancient Provençal Poets," a work notorious for its historical inaccuracies and fabrications.</note> utters nothing but fables regarding him. Among other things, he supposes him to be a gentleman of Orange who dedicated a treatise on the *Art of Loving* <note>original: "l’Art d’aimer"</note> to Princess Marguerite, who later became the wife of Louis IX. He adds that far from rewarding him, they exiled him to the Hyères Islands; but that he was recalled from his exile at the solicitation of Marguerite after she became Queen of France, and that he died in 1220. Thus, having died in 1220, he owed his recall, according to Nostradamus, to a queen who was not queen until 1234. This historian is just as accurate concerning the Countess of Die <note>Beatritz de Dia, a famous female troubadour (trobairitz) known for her songs of unrequited love.</note>.

The works of Rambaud number twenty-eight; those of the Countess number four.

## XIX.

# FOLQUET OF MARSEILLE,
### *Bishop of Toulouse.*

Folquet was the son of a merchant from Genoa, named Alphonse, who had settled in Marseille. Upon his death, he left his son master of a wealthy inheritance, at an age when riches most incite extravagance and pleasure. The young heir possessed a fiery imagination, which we shall see degenerate into fanaticism. <note>The author is likely referring to Folquet’s later role as Bishop of Toulouse, where he became a fierce and controversial leader in the Albigensian Crusade against the Cathars.</note> The labors of commerce could not please him; and in that era, opulence did not yet provide men of humble origin <term>hommes obscurs</term> <note>Literally "obscure men"; here it refers to those born outside the nobility, for whom wealth alone did not grant social prestige in the feudal hierarchy.</note> the means to distinguish themselves with brilliance. He preferred the service of the great and the role of a troubadour over the quiet and independent life that his fortune ensured him. Through this path, he gained free access to the greatest lords of his century. Richard I, King of Eng-

While this word often means "crimes" today, here it refers to his aggressive, bold maneuvers against the local nobility.</note>, Folquet traveled to Rome that same year, taking with him St. Dominic, whose order <note>The Dominican Order, also known as the Order of Preachers, founded to combat heresy through education and preaching.</note> had just been born in Toulouse. He presented him to the Pope; he vigorously requested the confirmation of this order, which was so formidable to the innovators <note>A derogatory term used by the Catholic Church to describe the Cathar heretics, implying they were "innovating" or inventing new, false doctrines.</note>. During the Lateran Council <note>The Fourth Lateran Council (1215), one of the most important councils in Church history, which dealt with the Crusades and the suppression of heresy.</note>, where Raymond appeared with his son and the Counts of Foix and Comminges, Folquet rose up against a cardinal who was speaking in their favor; and here is one of his reasons:

> "The Count of Foix cannot deny that his county is filled with heretics; for after the castle of Montségur <note>A famous mountain-top fortress and a major stronghold of the Cathars.</note> was taken, all the inhabitants were burned."

<summary>Bishop Folquet seizes the city of Toulouse and its palace, forcing Count Raymond into exile, before traveling to Rome with Saint Dominic to advocate for the newly formed Dominican Order at the Lateran Council.</summary>

Among the prelates <note>High-ranking church officials, such as bishops or abbots.</note> of this council, some wanted the dispossessed princes to be reinstated in their estates. The assemblies and judgments of the Church had indeed changed in nature!

One final detail will complete the portrait of Folquet and his hero, and the detestable spirit that wore the mask of religious zeal. Fanaticism did not even deign to respect the most basic duties of morality.

### XX.

## GIRAUD LE ROUX.

**Giraud le Roux**, according to our manuscript biographies, was born in Toulouse to a poor knight. For the penniless nobility of that era, there was no better course of action than to enter the service of a great lord. There, they found the benefits of education and the means of subsistence. While they might lose a certain degree of freedom, the spirit of chivalry <term>chivalry: the medieval system of knightly conduct and values, including honor, courtesy, and service</term> ennobled roles that seemed servile on the surface. These roles were considered honorable, not only at the courts of princes but also in the households of simple knights who were distinguished more by their merit than by their wealth. To serve them and to model oneself after their example were one and the same.

The young Giraud entered the service of the Count of Toulouse, Alphonse Jourdain <note>Alphonse Jourdain (1103–1148) was the Count of Toulouse and a significant patron of early troubadours; he was born in the Holy Land and named for the Jordan River.</note>,

<summary>This page introduces the troubadour Giraud le Roux, describing how the impoverished nobility of the 12th century sought education and advancement by serving in the courts of great lords.</summary>
<keywords>Giraud le Roux, Toulouse, Troubadours, Alphonse Jourdain, chivalry, nobility, medieval education, social hierarchy</keywords>

--- Page 330 ---
<meta>This page continues the biography of Giraud le Roux, detailing his life at the court of Alphonse Jourdain, Count of Toulouse, and the origins of his poetic career through his unrequited love for the Count's daughter.</meta>

<page-num>206</page-num>
<header>LITERARY HISTORY</header>

who had succeeded his brother Bertrand, who died in Syria in the year 1112. Flexible, obliging, diligent, and polite, he joined to these qualities a beautiful voice and the art of singing agreeably. These were infallible means of pleasing in a brilliant court. Unfortunately, with wit and grace, one felt entitled to the most reckless passions. Alphonse had a daughter, whom the Provençal historian does not name <note>original: "[ 1 ]"; It was common in the "Vidas" (biographies of troubadours) to leave the identity of the lady vague or protected by a pseudonym to maintain the codes of courtly love.</note>, whose charms made too great an impression on Giraud. He fell in love with her. Love made him a poet, as has happened so many times when sensitivity and talent were united. But his verses, written in a natural and tender style, speak only of the torments of an ill-fated love.

We have seven pieces by this <term>troubadour: a composer and performer of Old Occitan lyric poetry during the High Middle Ages</term>. In them, he lavishes praise upon the princess and finds in her every perfection, except that of having pity for her lover.

<summary>This page describes Giraud le Roux's rise in the court of Alphonse Jourdain through his musical talents and his subsequent unrequited love for the Count's daughter, which inspired his poetic works.</summary>

### XXI.

## BERTRAND DE BORN.

The memory of this illustrious <term>troubadour: a lyric poet and musician from southern France in the High Middle Ages, usually writing in Occitan on themes of courtly love and chivalry.</term> seems to have been at the mercy of the whims of fortune. An audacious warrior and politician, he is almost unknown to historians; a prolific and unique poet, he is likewise ignored in the annals of literature. So little solidity do brilliant reputations have, unless they are built upon either history written by excellent pens, or works worthy of serving as eternal models! That which shines even today can disappear a few days later. In the ages of darkness and poor taste, such was the natural order of human affairs.

BERTRAND DE BORN, Viscount of Hautefort <note>Hautefort is a commune in southwestern France, home to a famous fortress that was the center of Bertrand's many conflicts.</note> in the diocese of Péri- <note>The text breaks here; it refers to Périgord, a historical province in what is now the Dordogne department of France.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the troubadour Bertrand de Born, reflecting on how his historical and literary significance was neglected despite his prominence as both a warrior-nobleman and a poet.</summary>
<keywords>Bertrand de Born, troubadour, Hautefort, Périgord, literary history, medieval poetry, historical reputation</keywords>

--- Page 337 ---
<meta>This page continues the biography of Bertrand de Born, completing the name of the diocese of Périgueux from the previous page.</meta>

<page-num>211</page-num>

### OF THE TROUBADOURS.

gueux <note>This fragment completes the word "Périgueux," the seat of the diocese in the Périgord region of France.</note>, was one of the heroes of the twelfth century. A passion for arms and glory, pride joined with flexibility, gallantry joined with poetic talent, an ardent imagination and a lively spirit, much activity and courage along with a distinguished rank, put him in a position to distinguish himself in several careers. Our manuscripts provide us with the interesting details that we are about to report.

Justice ought to have characterized knights, if the maxims of <term>chivalry: the medieval institution of knighthood, which emphasized virtues such as courage, honor, and service.</term> had regulated their conduct. But Bertrand de Born, like almost all the brave men of old, was all the less acquainted with this virtue as he placed a higher value on the use of the sword. His brother Constantin shared with him the lordship of Hautefort <note>The Château de Hautefort is a massive fortress in the Dordogne; it was a site of constant siege and dispute during the Middle Ages.</note>, where there were about a thousand inhabitants. The ambitious Bertrand wanted to have everything. After long disputes, he ended by driving out his

But I declare it: he will regret it if he dares to contend with me. I will gouge out the eyes of whoever wishes to take my property from me. Peace does not suit me at all; war alone has the right to please me. To fear nothing: that is my only law. I have no regard for Mondays or Tuesdays <note>original: "ni aux lundis ni aux mardis." At all times, I wish to destroy anyone who harms me. Even if there were three of them, whatever their power may be, they will not win from me an inch of land (even the value of a leather strap)."

Richard, Count of Poitou <note>Later known as Richard the Lionheart.</note>, had a particular motive for vengeance. The revolts of the children of Henry II against their father are well known. After having wrested various <term>apanages: land or titles granted to the younger children of a monarch for their maintenance</term> from him, they fell out among themselves, and the king himself fomented their dissensions, which had become useful for his own peace of mind. Richard, fiery and greedy, had great disputes with Prince Henry, his elder brother, Duke of Guienne <note>The region of Aquitaine in southwestern France.</note> and crowned King of England in 1169 <note>Prince Henry was known as "The Young King" because he was crowned during his father's lifetime.</note>. Richard usurped Henry's rights; he made incursions onto his lands. The vassals took up arms for one or the other. Bertrand de Born was one of Richard's most dangerous enemies; Richard took revenge, as has been seen, by ransacking Bertrand's <term>seigneurie: the estate or territory over which a lord holds authority</term> in alliance with the Viscount of Limoges.

Bertrand was furious, in need of assistance, and stirred up enemies against him <note>Referring to Richard the Lionheart, who was then Count of Poitou.</note> from all sides. Since a great number of lords had cause to complain of the prince’s harassments, Bertrand soon formed a formidable league against him. After having succeeded so well through his intrigues, Bertrand employed the mechanisms of poetry. In former times among the Spartans and among our ancestors the Celts, poetry served to inspire martial ardor; it could still produce the same effect in a region where the imagination was as lively as the temperaments <note>The text here refers to the passionate nature of the people of Occitania (southern France).</note>

He had corrupted the Champenois <note>Knights and soldiers from the County of Champagne</note> within the enemy army through the use of money; he was counting on their desertion. Indeed, at the moment of joining battle, Philip found the Champenois alone to be resistant to his orders.
