Peace was established; Philip Augustus <note>Philip II of France, who reigned from 1180 to 1223</note> ceded Gisors <note>A strategic fortress on the border of Normandy and the French royal lands, long a point of contention</note>; the matter of homage <note>The formal act of a vassal acknowledging his king, which Richard had previously refused</note> remained unresolved.

The Provençal historian <note>Likely referring to the author of the *vidas*, the medieval biographies of the troubadours</note> adds that the two kings, having become frugal—and even miserly—no longer wished to assemble armies. They only incurred expenses to purchase land and to equip hunting parties. The barons viewed this peace with great distress, as it exposed them to the harassments of the kings' greed. Bertran de Born <note>c. 1140–1215; a celebrated soldier and troubadour famous for his "sirventes" or satirical songs that incited political conflict</note>, for whom war was his sole delight, was particularly distressed by this, especially since both his ambition and his fortune suffered as a result.

Consequently, he left no stone unturned in his efforts to rekindle the flames of discord. His satirical barbs made him a formidable figure to these sovereigns.

Maenz finally recognized the innocence of the troubadour, & restored her affection to him, requiring nonetheless (so serious were the affairs of love <note>The rules of "Courtly Love" in the 12th century were often as formal and legally minded as feudal law.</note>) that he go to take leave of Natibors, & in some way be released from his oath.

Maenz de Montagnac was courted by Richard, Count of Poitou <note>The future King Richard I of England, known as the Lionheart</note>, Geoffrey, Count of Brittany, Alfonso, King of Aragon, & Raymond, Count of Toulouse; yet she always preferred Bertrand de Born, whom she had chosen, says the Provençal historian, as her lover and her master.

<meta>This page continues the specific "Note" from page 248, which critiques the historical inaccuracies of a Provençal historian (Nostredame) regarding the lineage of the Counts of Barcelona and the Kings of Aragon.</meta>

<page-num>249</page-num>
<header>ON THE TROUBADOURS.</header>

and that this latter, having died in the town of Saint-Dalmas in Italy, left three sons: Alfonso (the same who had betrayed Bertran de Born), Sancho, and Berenguer of Besalú. The opposite is attested by all other historical records. The House of the Counts of Barcelona descended in a direct line from Wilfred the Hairy <note>Geofroi le Velu, the 9th-century count credited with establishing the hereditary nature of the County of Barcelona</note>, the first proprietary count of Catalonia, who died in 912.

Here is what may have given rise to the error of the Provençal historian. It appears certain that Gilbert, Count of Provence and successor to Bertrand, was the son of a Count of Milhaud in Rouergue, who may have been this Pierre de Carlad of whom we have just spoken. It also appears that Almodis, the second wife of Ramon Berenguer III, Count of Barcelona, was the sister of Count Gilbert; however, she died without children. Ramon Berenguer then married Princess Douce, the daughter of Gilbert, as his third wife. Thus, the Counts of Barcelona, who succeeded Ramon, drew their origin from Pierre de Carlad through the maternal line. It does not follow that Alfonso was of humble extraction. The historian also shows little judgment in saying that Ramon Berenguer IV, who married the heiress of Aragon, was the son of Pierre de Carlad: he

### X X I I.

## GUILLAUME RAINOLS
## OF APT.

Guillaume Rainols, according to our manuscripts, was a knight from the town of Apt in the county of Forcalquier. He composed good <term>sirventes<note>The sirventes was a specific genre of troubadour poetry. Unlike the "canso," which focused on courtly love, the sirventes was typically used for political satire, moralizing, or personal attacks.</note></term> regarding the events taking place in Provence between the King of Aragon and the Count of Toulouse. He composed new melodies for each of his sirventes; and since they were all biting, he made himself formidable to all the barons because of them. Indeed, his <term>causticity<note>A sharp, biting, or sarcastic wit.</note></term> is evident in several of his surviving pieces.

We do not possess those works which concerned the King of Aragon (Alfonso) and the Count of Toulouse (Raymond V). They dealt with the marriage of Douce, heiress of Provence, to the son of Raymond. <note>The King of Aragon mentioned is Alfonso II (reigned 1162–1196), and the Count is Raymond V of Toulouse (reigned 1148–1194). The marriage of Douce II, Countess of Provence, was a central point of contention in the "Great War of the South," a struggle for territorial control between the houses of Barcelona and Toulouse.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the 12th-century troubadour Guillaume Rainols of Apt, describing him as a knight and a writer of sharp political satires who was feared by the nobility for his scathing wit.</summary>
<keywords>Guillaume Rainols, Apt, Forcalquier, sirventes, Provence, Aragon, Toulouse, Alfonso II, Raymond V, Douce of Provence</keywords>

The <term>sirvente<note>A genre of troubadour lyric poetry, often satirical or political in nature, used to comment on social or moral issues.</note></term> I am about to describe must have been composed at the beginning of the following century, when the crusade against the <term>Albigensians<note>A dualist religious movement in Southern France that was declared heretical by the Catholic Church, leading to a decades-long military campaign known as the Albigensian Crusade (1209–1229).</note></term> was engulfing the southern regions of France. The <term>troubadour<note>A composer and performer of Old Occitan lyric poetry during the High Middle Ages.</note></term> lashes out against the clergy, to whom so many acts of violence and injustice were attributed.

# XXIII.

## GUILLAUME & RAIMOND DE DURFORT.

The castle of Durfort in Quercy <note>Quercy is a former province in southwestern France, centered around Cahors.</note> gave its name to this illustrious House of Durfort, one of the oldest surviving in the monarchy, one of those which has branched out into the most lineages, and where nobility of character has best sustained the grandeur of its origin. Two troubadours <term>troubadour: A composer and performer of Old Occitan lyric poetry during the High Middle Ages, typically focusing on themes of courtly love and chivalry.</term> emerged from this family; for it appears that Guillaume and Raimond are not the same person, since different pieces are found under the two names. The only one we have from Guillaume is very obscure, due to the constraints of the rhymes and the corruption of the text. It is addressed to the Lord of Périgord, and contains the praise of one Gui Cap-de-Porc <note>original: "Gui Cap-de-Porc." This name literally translates to "Guy Pig-Head," which may have been a nickname or a specific family branch name.</note>, an unknown lord. The poet [describes] him:

...praises [him] for loving honor and for being courageous against vices, for having no need for external ornaments because he shines through his virtues. "Would that we all resembled him! What vexes me is that he does not have as many marks <note>A "mark" was a unit of weight for gold and silver, worth significantly more than a denier.</note> as he has pennies <note>original: "deniers." The denier was a small medieval coin of low value.</note>; for he would gild those whom others leaden: (he would enrich those whom others crush.)" <note>The original French play on words contrasts "doreroit" (would gild/enrich) with "plombent" (to leaden/strike down).</note> These traits announce a noble writer, superior to the prejudices as well as the vices of his century. The same sentiments still exist, I dare to assert, in the descendants of his lineage.

Two *sirventes* <term>sirventes: A genre of Old Occitan lyric poetry used by troubadours, typically for satirical, political, or moral themes rather than courtly love.</term> by *Raimond*, composed jointly with *Tuex*, *Malet*, and *Cornils*, knights of *Quercy*, are unintelligible. Crescimbeni <note>Giovanni Mario Crescimbeni (1663–1728) was an Italian critic and historian of poetry.</note> speaks of *Raimond* de *Durfort*, whom he says was a contemporary of *Arnaud Daniel* <note>Arnaut Daniel was a famous 12th-century troubadour, famously praised by Dante as the "best smith of the mother tongue."</note>.

### XXIV.

## RAMBAUD DE VAQUEIRAS
## or VACHEIRAS.

Rambaud de Vaqueiras was the son of a knight named Peirols, from Vachères <note>Vachères is a small village in the modern-day Alpes-de-Haute-Provence region of France.</note> in the principality of Orange. Lacking in financial fortune, he possessed the talent to acquire it. Even in those times, it was already a true misfortune that talent could hardly prosper except through the sacrifice of precious liberty. But we shall see that Vaqueiras wrote in the courts as a free man. He first attached himself—in the capacity of a *jongleur* <term>jongleur: A wandering entertainer or minstrel who performed the songs of troubadours, often playing instruments and sometimes performing acrobatics.</term> and undoubtedly as a *troubadour* <term>troubadour: A medieval lyric poet and musician from southern France who wrote in the Occitan language, primarily on themes of courtly love and chivalry.</term>—to Guillaume de Baux <note>William I of Baux (c. 1155–1218), who became Prince of Orange in 1182.</note>, first Prince of Orange, whose subject he was.

As early as the year 971, the House of Baux was known as one of the most illustrious in the county of Arles. It disputed toward the middle

> ...Spain <note>The text continues from the previous page's mention of a horse from Spain.</note>, impatient and held back for too long. He routed a company of three strangers joined together. But I heard no one pity them, because they had come there from a foreign land.

A description of a tournament in the works of Ariosto <note>Ludovico Ariosto (1474–1533), the Italian poet famous for his epic *Orlando Furioso*, known for his highly romanticized depictions of chivalry.</note> would charm the imagination with poetic imagery; this one may interest the reader through the tone of mockery that distinguishes it. The poet seems to have viewed this grand spectacle only through a ridiculous lens.

The troubadours <note>Medieval lyric poets from southern France who wrote in Occitan, often focusing on themes of courtly love and chivalry.</note> loved to wander the world, much like the knights. From the court of the Prince of Orange, Vaqueiras <note>Rambaud de Vaqueiras (c. 1165–1207), a celebrated troubadour and knight who spent much of his career in the service of Boniface of Montferrat.</note> went to Italy to join Boniface, Marquis of Montferrat. We shall see him play a major role there. While passing through Genoa, he became acquainted with a woman whose heart he wished to win, but whom he found inflexible. This is the subject of a <term>tenson</term> <note>tenson: A poetic debate or dialogue between two speakers, common in troubadour literature, often used to argue points of love or ethics.</note>, a simple dialogue, in which he expresses himself thus:

The coarse simplicity of this dialogue is a reflection of the customs of the time, which, even in the courts and in the company of the muses, retained a foundation of rusticity. The poet portrays his Genoese woman as very impolite; but he does not conceal the opinion held in Italy regarding the Provençals <note>Troubadours from Southern France who spoke the Occitan language, often called "Provençal" at the time.</note>, whose excesses in the Kingdom of Naples later only increased the hatred of the Italians.

Boniface, Marquis of Montferrat, was an enlightened and generous benefactor to him. According to our historian, Vaqueiras perfected himself so much at his court, in the art of war as in poetry, that he earned great esteem. These two talents were the admiration of the Marquis. He accepted the command, traveled to France where he took the cross <note>To "take the cross" was the formal ceremony of vowing to join a crusade, marked by the wearing of a cross on one's garments.</note>, and planned the enterprise with the leading lords of the land.

### X X V.

## THE DAUPHIN OF AUVERGNE & THE BISHOP OF CLERMONT.

Where did the title of **Dauphin** <note>The word "Dauphin" literally means "dolphin" in French. While later associated with the heirs to the French throne, it began as a personal name and then a title for the rulers of the Viennois and Auvergne regions.</note> come from; & how was it transmitted from the House of Vienne to that of Auvergne? These questions are of little interest to the history of the troubadours; but the nature of our work allows us to clarify them in a few words.

The tournaments, where each lord bore a distinctive mark on his shield <note>original: "écu"</note>, probably gave rise to the title in question. A Count of Albon had taken a dolphin for an emblem. He distinguished himself in the tournaments. People praised the "knight of the dolphin" <note>original: "le chevalier du dauphin"</note>. The custom soon prevailed of calling him simply the **Dauphin**; & this famous name became a title of dignity for his descendants.

<vocab>Dauphin, Auvergne, Clermont, Vienne, Albon, troubadours, tournaments, emblem, shield</vocab>

<summary>This page explains the heraldic origins of the title "Dauphin," tracing it back to a Count of Albon who used a dolphin emblem in medieval tournaments.</summary>
<keywords>Dauphin of Auvergne, heraldry, House of Albon, tournaments, origins of titles, medieval history</keywords>

--- Page 438 ---
<meta>This page continues the genealogical explanation of the title "Dauphin," tracing its movement from the House of Vienne to the House of Auvergne through marriage and an inheritance dispute.</meta>

<page-num>304</page-num>
<header>LITERARY HISTORY</header>

[The title] passed into the house of Auvergne, according to Baluze and Charier *, through a daughter of Guigues III, Count of Albon and Vienne, who married William VII, Count of Auvergne. The latter, having been dispossessed of his rights—contrary to the laws of representation <note>In inheritance law, the "right of representation" allows the children of a deceased heir to claim their parent's share of an estate.</note>—by William VIII, his uncle, held only a considerable appanage <note>An "appanage" was a grant of land or money given to members of a noble family who did not inherit the primary title, intended to provide for their maintenance.</note>, which he passed to his descendants; his son was the first to bear the name of **Dauphin**, and this new title distinguished his branch from that of William VIII.

The **DAUPHIN OF AUVERGNE** is the same troubadour of whom we have already spoken in the article on Richard, King of England <note>Richard the Lionheart (1157–1199), who was himself a poet and a patron of troubadours.</note>. We have seen their quarrels, and the poetic pieces they wrote against one another. Our manuscripts provide us with other facts and other curious excerpts.

---

\* Baluze, *History of Auvergne*; Charier, *History of the Dauphiné*.

<summary>This page describes how the title of Dauphin was inherited by the Counts of Auvergne and notes that the Dauphin of Auvergne was a famous troubadour who exchanged satirical poems with King Richard the Lionheart.</summary>
<keywords>House of Auvergne, Guigues III, William VII, William VIII, inheritance law, Richard the Lionheart, troubadour poetry, genealogy</keywords>

They represent the dauphin <note>Robert I, Count of Clermont (c. 1150–1234), known as the Dauphin of Auvergne.</note> as an accomplished knight; the best in arms and in love; the most courteous, the most sensible; who knew best how to compose *sirventes* <term>sirventes: satirical or political songs used by troubadours to comment on current events or personal rivalries</term>, couplets, airs, and *tensons* <term>tensons: a type of poetic debate or "contest" between two poets, usually regarding themes of love or philosophy</term>; who spoke, finally, with the greatest judgment and grace. An emulator and protector of poets, he attracted them in crowds to his side, honored them, and showered them with wealth. Hugues Brunet, Pierre d’Auvergne, and Perdigon <note>Famous troubadours of the 12th and 13th centuries.</note> shared significantly in his favors.

The wisdom attributed to him by the Provençal historian <note>A reference to the authors of the "Vidas," the semi-biographical accounts of the troubadours written in the Occitan (Provençal) language.</note> does not align with either a ruinous prodigality or an unjust rapacity. However, after having lost more than half of his wealth through lavish spending, he recovered or amassed even more, it is said, through his shrewdness and his avarice. The magnificence from which he had gained too much honor led him to a dishonorable excess: for the morals of that time stigmatized avarice above all else, and seemed to put

[The title] passed into the house of Auvergne, according to Baluze <note>Étienne Baluze (1630–1718), a renowned French scholar and historian of the Auvergne region.</note> and Charier*, through a daughter of Guigues III, count of Albon and of Vienne, who married William VII, count of Auvergne. The latter, having been dispossessed against the right of representation <term>right of representation: a legal principle where a descendant takes the place of a deceased ancestor in the line of inheritance</term> by William VIII, his uncle, received only a considerable appanage <term>appanage: a grant of land or money given to younger members of a noble family for their support</term>, which he passed on to his descendants; his son was the first to bear the name of **Dauphin** <note>original: "Dauphin." While the word literally means "dolphin," it became a prestigious title in this region, eventually giving its name to the province of Dauphiné.</note>, and this new title distinguished his branch of the family from that of William VIII.

The **DAUPHIN OF AUVERGNE** is the same troubadour of whom we have already spoken in the article on Richard, King of England <note>Richard I, known as the Lionheart, who was also a poet and patron of the arts.</note>. Their quarrels have already been seen, as well as the poems they wrote against one another. Our manuscripts provide us with other facts and other curious excerpts.

At the beginning of the poem, he claimed to be impatiently awaiting the papal legate <note>A personal representative of the Pope with the authority to act on his behalf.</note> in order to have the Bishop deposed. In the heat of passion, nothing is easier than to contradict oneself.

In other respects, Robert, Bishop of Clermont, deserved severe criticism for his behavior. ### XXVI.

## BERTRAND DE LA TOUR.

A single stanza by the Dauphin of Auvergne <note>The Dauphin of Auvergne (c. 1150–1234) was both a powerful feudal lord and a notable troubadour known for his biting wit.</note> against BERTRAND DE LA TOUR, and his response to the Dauphin, constitute the entire subject of this entry. These consist of mutual reproaches regarding their way of life.

The former <note>The Dauphin.</note> reproaches the latter <note>Bertrand.</note>, stating that despite having been wealthy, powerful, courageous, esteemed, and having traveled far from his homeland, he now shuts himself away in his castle with his goshawks and his falcons; and that when he has twenty people at his house, he believes he is hosting a grand festival for Christmas or Easter.

Bertrand responds that it would be in poor taste for him to live in any other manner while the Dauphin sets the example of an even more secluded life; following the proverb: *Like master, like man* <note>original: "Tel est le maître, tel doit être le valet"—literally: "As is the master, so must be the servant."</note>.

## XXVII.

### DEUDES DE PRADES.

Deudes de Prades, so named for the place of his birth in Rouergue <note>A historic province in the south of France, now primarily the department of Aveyron.</note>, was a canon of Maguelone <note>The Cathedral of Maguelone was a significant religious and political center located on an island near Montpellier.</note>. A man of wisdom, wit, and letters, who composed well according to our manuscript histories, he nevertheless enjoyed little success in the world; his songs were poorly received there because they were not inspired by love.

What does the Provençal <term>Provençal: Refers here to the Occitan language and the literary tradition of the troubadours of southern France.</term> historian mean? Around twenty pieces that remain to us from this troubadour are full of gallantry and amorous sentiments; moreover, they are written with more elegance than many others whose authors achieved great reputations. Deudes apparently lived far from the courts—that theater where poetic talents went to seek both...

## XXVIII.

### PEYROLS OF AUVERGNE.

This troubadour was a knight without fortune, from the castle of Peyrols in the lands of the Dauphin of Auvergne <note>The "Dauphin of Auvergne" was a title used by the rulers of the county of Clermont to distinguish their lineage from the Counts of Auvergne.</note>, at the foot of Roquefort. Through his politeness, his gentleness, and an agreeable appearance, he won the favor of the Dauphin, who retained him in his service; he provided him with horses, arms, and clothing, and let him want for nothing.

A sister of this prince, the wife of Bernard de Mercœur <note>The House of Mercœur was one of the most powerful baronial families in the Auvergne region during the Middle Ages.</note>, a great baron of Auvergne, possessed charms with which Peyrols fell in love. Flattered to be the subject of his songs, she was not, moreover, indifferent to his love; but vanity initially led her to reject the advances of a man so far beneath her station.

The Countess of Mercœur, half-conquered by a secret passion, willingly yielded to the urgings of the Dauphin <note>Robert I, Dauphin of Auvergne (c. 1150–1234), was himself a celebrated troubadour and a patron of the arts.</note>, who entreated her on behalf of the troubadour. ->**OF THE TROUBADOURS.**<-

His fickleness in love appears in a <term>tenson (a poetic debate between two troubadours)</term>, where he asks the <term>Dauphin of Auvergne (Robert I, a count and noted patron of poets)</term> if a lover ought to love his mistress more after having obtained everything from her <note>In the context of courtly love, "obtaining everything" refers to the physical consummation of the relationship.</note>. The Dauphin responds that fulfillment should increase love. Peyrols says, on the contrary, that it extinguishes pure and perfect love. The tenderness of a true lover, according to the Dauphin, only grows warmer through gratitude; and it is only an uncourtly lover who grows cold toward his lady once she has left him nothing more to desire. 

"I do not know," Peyrols responds. "In any case, I advise him, if he no longer loves her as much, to always pretend to love her even more." 

"I see," says the Dauphin, "that you judge the hearts of others by your own, which is worth nothing."

The final tensons still revolve around these fulfillments, more or less frequent, more or less disputed; material worthy of a <term>libertine (socially or morally unrestrained)</term> pen.

<summary>This page describes a poetic debate between the troubadour Peyrols and the Dauphin of Auvergne regarding whether physical intimacy strengthens or weakens love. Peyrols takes a cynical, "libertine" stance, suggesting that desire fades after fulfillment, while the Dauphin defends the ideals of courtly gratitude.</summary>

### XXIX.

## ALBERT, *Marquis of Malaspina.*

ALBERT was of the house of the Marquises of *Malaspina*, one of the most illustrious of *Lombardy*. Our manuscripts depict him as a valiant, courteous, liberal <note>In the medieval courtly context, "liberal" (largesse) referred to the essential virtue of being generous with one's wealth, particularly toward poets and performers.</note>, well-learned, and a good troubadour. *Bembo*, *Mario Equicola*, and *Crescimbeni* <note>These were prominent Italian humanists and literary historians of the 15th and 16th centuries who sought to document the origins of Italian poetry.</note> have celebrated him and placed him among the principal poets of his time. He flourished toward the end of the twelfth century, being a contemporary of *Raimbaut de Vaqueiras*. A very curious <term>tenson (a poetic debate or exchange between two troubadours)</term> with the latter serves as proof of this.

The Marquis Albert asks *Raimbaut* if it is true that he was dismissed by a mistress for whom he had written songs in vain, and who had attacked him in a <term>sirventes (a satirical or critical poem, usually on political or personal themes)</term>?

It highlights his historical connection to the famous poet Raimbaut de Vaqueiras through a surviving poetic debate.</summary>

## XXIX.

### ALBERT, *Marquis of Malaspina.*

Albert belonged to the house of the Marquises of Malaspina, one of the most illustrious in Lombardy <note>A region in Northern Italy known for its powerful noble families and patronage of the arts.</note>. Our manuscripts depict him as a man of valor, courtesy, and liberality, well-educated and a skilled <term>troubadour (a medieval poet-musician of noble or professional status)</term>. Bembo, Marius Equicola, and Crescimbeni <note>Pietro Bembo, Mario Equicola, and Giovanni Mario Crescimbeni were famous Italian scholars who wrote extensively on the history of poetry and the Italian language.</note> have celebrated him and placed him among the principal poets of his time. He flourished toward the end of the twelfth century, being a contemporary of Rambaud de Vaqueiras. A very curious <term>tenson (a poetic debate or competition between two troubadours)</term> with the latter serves as proof of this.

The Marquis Albert asks Rambaud if it is true that he has been dismissed by a mistress, for whom he had composed songs in vain, and who had attacked him in a <term>sirventes (a satirical or personal song, often used to mock or criticize)</term>?

## OGIER or AUGIER.

This <term>troubadour</term> <note>A lyric poet and performer of the High Middle Ages who wrote in the Occitan language.</note> is named in our manuscripts as Ogier, Ogiers of Vienne, Augier, and Ugier of Saint-Donat, a town in the <term>Viennois</term> <note>A historical region in southeastern France, surrounding the city of Vienne.</note>. He resided for a long time in Lombardy; he composed good <term>tensons</term> <note>original: "tensons"; a poetic debate or "contention" between two poets.</note> and good <term>sirventes</term> <note>original: "sirventes"; a genre of troubadour poetry often focused on satire, politics, or moralizing rather than courtly love.</note>, in which he praised some and blamed others. His pieces prove that he flourished toward the end of the twelfth century. The first that presents itself is bristling with wordplay and full of bizarre rhymes, resulting in as much obscurity as bad taste. <note>The author here critiques the "Trobar Ric" or "Trobar Clus" styles, which favored complex technical skill and intentional difficulty over simple clarity.</note>

### XXXI.

## ELIAS DE BARJOLS.

ELIAS, born in Payols in the Agenais region <note>A historical region in southwest France, centered around the city of Agen.</note>, was the son of a merchant. (Nostradamus <note>Jean de Nostredame, whose 1575 work "Lives of the Most Celebrated and Ancient Provençal Poets" is known for blending historical fact with creative invention.</note> claims he was a nobleman.) He possessed wit and a beautiful voice. The profession of a jongleur <term>jongleur: a traveling entertainer who performed music, storytelling, and the poems of troubadours at court.</term> seemed preferable to him over trade; and he partnered with a certain Olivier to practice it. They were soon seen in the royal courts. Alfonso II, Count of Provence, whose reign began in 1196 and ended in 1209, secured their loyalty through generous provisions. He arranged marriages for them and gave them lands at Barjols in the diocese of Riez, from which Elias took his name "de Barjols."

After the death of the Count, he fell in love with his widow, Garsende de Sabran, who was, according to our manuscripts, the subject of his songs for as long as he lived.

<sig>P vij</sig>

<vocab>Elias de Barjols, Payols, Agenais, Nostradamus, Alfonso II, Provence, Barjols, Riez, Garsende de Sabran, troubadours, jongleur</vocab>

<summary>This page introduces the troubadour Elias de Barjols, a merchant's son who became a court favorite under Alfonso II of Provence and famously dedicated his songs to the Count's widow, Garsende de Sabran.</summary>

> » In what have I offended you, Love?
> » Must the beautiful lady, the sole object of
> » my vows, disdain me and kill me?
> » It is you who are the cause of it. However,
> » Love, after having tormented me so much,
> » it would be fitting to grant me a
> » fine pleasure from the beauty I adore.
> » If I die for having desired this
> » blessing in vain, she will eternally regret
> » the refusal of a slight favor,
> » which could have saved my life.
> » Like a poor man, whose extreme need
> » causes him to solicit a meager aid,
> » it would suffice for me that for a single day, through your
> » power, my prayers might touch her
> » who deals me death.
> » But you do not wish it to be
> » said that such bliss was the
> » reward for my painful constancy. <term>constancy: the courtly virtue of remaining faithful to one's lady regardless of her coldness or the passage of time.</term>

# XXXII.

## GAUCELM FAIDIT.

This troubadour is one of those whose biography is among the longest in our manuscripts—that is to say, one whose romantic adventures are recorded with the most detail; for the Provençal historian <note>A reference to the authors of the *Vidas*, the traditional prose biographies of troubadours preserved in medieval songbooks</note> loves to dwell on such matters and always passes lightly over others.

Gaucelm Faidit was the son of a bourgeois <note>In this context, a member of the merchant or urban middle class, rather than a noble</note> from Uzerche, a town in the diocese of Limoges. He lived a very libertine youth and ruined himself through a passion for gambling. Lacking any other resources, he took up the profession of an actor <note>original: "histrion," a term often used for stage performers or mimes</note> and a minstrel <note>original: "jongleur," a traveling entertainer who performed songs and poetry</note>. Everything he earned, he squandered on fine dining, eating and drinking to such excess that he became immoderately fat. He married a public woman <note>A prostitute</note> from the town of Alest (undoubtedly Alais).

<summary>This page introduces the biography of Gaucelm Faidit, a troubadour from Uzerche who turned to life as a traveling performer after losing his wealth to gambling and excess.</summary>
<keywords>Gaucelm Faidit, troubadour, Uzerche, Limoges, jongleur, medieval biography, gambling, Alais</keywords>

He traveled the world for twenty years without a reputation, and consequently without finding much of a welcome. At last, he acquired the name of troubadour; and the success of his songs led him to be sought out by Richard, Count of Poitou, son of Henry II, King of England, and his successor in 1189 <note>Known to history as Richard the Lionheart</note>. Faidit must have still been very young, judging by a piece in his collection which could only have been composed in 1260 <note>The author notes a chronological difficulty here; Gaucelm Faidit is generally believed to have died around 1202. The ambition to make illustrious conquests in love equaled the desire to shine through poetic talent at that time. Faidit had the audacity to address his vows <note>In the tradition of courtly love, "vows" (vœux) were formal declarations of romantic devotion</note> to her. She appeared sensitive to them, as almost all ladies did in such cases in order to become the heroines of a troubadour; but he soon perceived that the reality did not match appearances.

In several songs, he complains of the harshness of his lady; he implores her pity, and conjures her not to let him die; he says that she has made him out of nothing; that he must thank her for it; yet he would prefer to obtain some gift from her; he compares her to the tarantula <note>A reference to the medieval belief that the bite of a tarantula caused "tarantism," a state of uncontrollable laughter or dancing leading to death</note> who causes death while laughing; he even wishes that a deceitful lover might avenge him, and punish her for refusing a submissive and sincere lover; nonetheless, he does not cease to protest that he will always love her, even though he knows it is a folly.

Finally he set sail. Having arrived in the Holy Land <note>The Eastern Mediterranean region where the Crusaders fought to reclaim Jerusalem</note>, still preoccupied with his lady, he sang that she had made him cross the sea, that he burned with the desire to return, and that a rival was being preferred over him. More a lover than a warrior, he hastened his return. His efforts of obedience seemed to him worthy enough to be soon rewarded.

But he found his mistress more severe than ever. At first, he complained of this in song; comparing himself to a man plunged to the bottom of the sea, from which he cannot be pulled out, and where he cannot remain without dying. Despair then led him to an extreme resolution. He presented himself with a troubled air to Marie de Ventadour. "Madame," he said to her, "you see a lover beside himself, too overwhelmed by your rigors <note>In the tradition of courtly love, "rigors" refers to the lady's coldness or refusal to grant her favor to the poet</note>. This speech, though likely invented by the **Provençal** <note>This refers to the medieval biographers who wrote "Vidas," or life stories of the troubadours, which often blended historical fact with romantic legend</note> historian, captures the natural simplicity that was then joined with **gallantry** <note>A refined code of conduct in medieval courts involving polite behavior, wit, and romantic devotion</note>. Such an engaging proposal, combined with the lady's beauty and her amorous glances, made such an impression on the soul of the poet that he was at first beside himself. Having regained his composure, he expressed his deepest gratitude to her and promised to submit to her wishes, to give himself to her, and to sing of no one but her. The lady received him courteously, but chilled him with her response. After vague compliments on his merit, she declared to him that she had never had the will to love him with *love* <note>original: 'amour'; in the context of troubadour poetry, this specifically refers to "fin'amor" or courtly romantic love, distinguished here from platonic friendship</note>; that she had only wanted to rescue him from slavery <note>The "slavery" of love was a common poetic theme where the poet is a "servant" to a demanding lady</note>, and dissipate the foolish hopes in which he had languished for more than seven years; that moreover, without being his mistress, she would always be his friend, and very eager to do whatever else he might wish.

These words were a thunderbolt for the troubadour. He cried for mercy to the lady, imploring her not to betray, deceive, and kill him in such a way.

# ON THE TROUBADOURS.

Boniface, Marquis of Montferrat, also loved the muses <note>A classical reference to the goddesses of the arts, meaning the Marquis was a patron of poetry.</note>. Faidit was at his court for some time: he often designates him in his verses as the *valiant marquis* <note>original: "preux marquis"</note>. He finally settled at the court of Raimond d’Agoult, Lord of Sault, one of the greatest lords of Provence. After so many heartaches caused by love, one would not expect to see him in love once more: he was, however, and he even had a prince for a rival.

Lady Jordana de Brun, a noble and very amiable woman, lived in a castle at the far edge of Provence, on the border of Lombardy. Faidit declared himself her lover; and he brought her such honor, says the historian, served her so well, and so often begged for mercy, that she made him her knight even though he was not a man of noble birth <note>In the tradition of "courtly love," a poet could be symbolically knighted by his lady as a sign of her favor, regardless of his actual social rank.</note>. In his songs, he always calls her his *fair hope* <note>original: "bel espoir"</note>.

### XXXIII.

## ELIAS CAIRELS.

Although this troubadour was unknown to Nostradamus <note>Jehan de Nostredame (1507–1577), the younger brother of the famous astrologer, who wrote a famous but often unreliable biographical collection of troubadour lives.</note>, and although our manuscripts do not agree on his account, he provides several curious details for our history.

**ELIAS CAIRELS** was born in Sarlat in Périgord. His first profession was working in gold and silver, and designing coats of arms. Whether out of whim, ambition, or an irresistible inclination, he dedicated himself to the Muses as a minstrel <term>jongleur: an itinerant performer who sang, played instruments, and sometimes performed acts of skill, often reciting the works of troubadours</term> and troubadour; but his hopes for success were dashed. According to one of our historians, he composed, sang, and played the fiddle poorly; he spoke even worse; and his talent was limited to copying tunes and lyrics well. According to another, he was learned in literature;

<summary>This page introduces Elias Cairels, a former goldsmith and heraldic designer from Sarlat who transitioned into the life of a troubadour, despite conflicting historical accounts of his musical and poetic talent.</summary>
<keywords>Elias Cairels, Sarlat, Périgord, troubadour, jongleur, Jehan de Nostredame, heraldry, medieval biography</keywords>

--- Page 533 ---
<meta>This page continues the biography of the troubadour Elias Cairels, contrasting two different manuscript accounts of his skill and his travels.</meta>

<header>OF THE TROUBADOURS.</header>

...composed, recited, and performed with great talent everything he wished; yet he did not succeed as much as his works deserved, because he despised the world and the lords. The first manuscript asserts that he spent a long time in Romania <note>In the Middle Ages, "Romania" typically referred to the Latin Empire of Constantinople or the broader Byzantine territories where many troubadours traveled during the Crusades.</note>, and that he returned to Sarlat, where he died; the second, that he traveled across most of the inhabited world. His works provide clearer insights into the era and circumstances of his life.

We possess sixteen of his pieces. He was one of those poets who took pleasure in multiplying the technical difficulties of the art, for the honor of overcoming them. Short verses and sophisticated rhymes <term>rimes recherchées: elaborate and rare rhyming patterns intended to showcase a poet's technical mastery</term> seemed to him of great merit, as did the practice of beginning each stanza with the final words of the previous one. He harshly accuses those who prefer a simple song in easy rhymes of having bad taste. Regarding such trivialities, a writer

This refers to Frederick II, Emperor from the year 1220. This prince, as we shall see elsewhere, loved and cultivated poetry. The troubadour had undoubtedly attached himself to his service. If he left dissatisfied, it was perhaps because he expected too much from the Emperor’s generosity, or because he deserved it too little. <note>Frederick II was known as a great patron of the arts, suggesting the poet's complaints might stem from personal failure rather than the Emperor's stinginess.</note>

Whether these invectives <note>Referring to the sharp poetic criticisms by Elias Cairels mentioned on the previous page.</note> had any influence or not, William finally determined in 1224 to attempt the conquest of the kingdom of Thessalonica <note>The Kingdom of Thessalonica was a short-lived Crusader state founded after the Fourth Crusade (1204).</note>, of which his brother Demetrius had been stripped, as was mentioned above. But if he despised the world and the lords, as one of our manuscripts observes; if he lacked the supple character of a courtier, or a genius for intrigue, as his works seem to prove; then even with greater merit, he likely would have failed in the courts. They have always been the stumbling block for rigid minds, even more so than for virtuous souls.

This poet shows, however, much ambition through a piece in which he explains his desires. He asks for gold, silver, and cattle; the wisdom of Solomon, the courtesy of Roland <note>Roland, the legendary paladin of Charlemagne, was the medieval archetype of bravery and knightly decorum.</note>, the power of Alexander <note>Alexander the Great was frequently invoked in medieval literature as a symbol of worldly power and "largesse" (generosity).</note>, the strength of Samson, the lady-love of Tristan <note>A reference to Iseult; the romance of Tristan and Iseult was one of the most influential stories of courtly love.</note>, the chivalry of Gawain <note>Gawain was celebrated in Arthurian legend as the most courteous and skilled of the Knights of the Round Table.</note>, and the knowledge of Merlin; he seeks a loyalty so perfect that no knight and no jongleur <note>A jongleur was a professional performer who traveled to courts to sing, play instruments, and recite poetry.</note>...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of Elias Cairels' contradictory character, specifically contrasting the humble life of a poet with his extravagant, almost royal, fantasies.</meta>

might find nothing to reproach in him; a mistress young, pretty, and respectable <note>The original French "décente" refers to a lady who adheres to the proper social and moral codes of courtly love.</note>; a thousand knights in good order to follow him everywhere: these are his desires. Finally, he wishes to always find merchandise for sale, and to always have the means to buy everything. For he would like to constantly receive a great company and be able to host them well without it costing anyone anything.

How can these wishes be reconciled with his contempt for the world and for lords? Unless we say that Elias Cairels envied fortune by inclination, and despised out of pride or spite those whom he saw enjoying it. The truly wise man knows better how to be content with his lot: it is by moderating his desires that he places himself above wealth and greatness.

### XXXIV.

## BERTRAND D’ALAMANON.

We are forced, against our will, to turn to *Nostradamus* <note>Jean de Nostredame (c. 1522–1576), younger brother of the famous astrologer Michel de Nostredame. His "Lives of the Ancient Provençal Poets" is often criticized for its historical inaccuracies and embellishments.</note> for the life of this *troubadour*, as our Provençal manuscripts contain only his works. Few historians, undoubtedly, deserve less confidence; but here at least, he will not be seen in contradiction with others.

Bertrand, the son and grandson of lords of the same name, held the fief of Alamanon (today Lamanon), in the diocese of Aix in Provence. A gentleman of the most considerable standing in the country, he distinguished himself singularly among the poets. He had as his mistress Fanette or Étiennette de Gantelmi, Lady of Romanin, who then held, says *Nostradamus*, a court of lo- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; it refers to a "cour d'amour" or Court of Love, a historical concept of a tribunal where ladies debated and judged matters of courtly romance.</note>

-ve <note>original: "mour", completing "cour d'amour" or "court of love" from the previous page.</note> at her castle. We have proven that these courts of love did not yet exist <note>The author is refuting Jean de Nostredame’s claim that formal "Courts of Love"—tribunals where noblewomen judged romantic disputes—existed during this period; most modern scholars agree they were a literary invention.</note>; but let us continue to follow the author, without pausing for a critique. The Lady of Romanin was the aunt of the famous Laura, immortalized by the poet Petrarch. Alamanon composed beautiful songs in her honor. He eventually grew weary of love, for reasons unknown, and devoted himself to a taste for satire directed against princes.

Satire has had its dangers in every age: it excites hatred, and hatred inspires vengeance. The troubadour did not even spare Charles II of Anjou, King of Naples and Count of Provence, whose subject he was. Consequently, Charles took his revenge by stripping Alamanon of a hereditary right belonging to his house: the duty on the salt that passed over the bridge of the Durance at Pertuis <note>Pertuis is a town in the Vaucluse department; the Durance river was a major trade route where tolls and salt taxes (gabelles) were lucrative rights for local lords.</note>. This act of authority triggered new satires, which could only serve to worsen the conflict.

Fortunately for the satirist, he then exercised his talent against the enemies of the King of Naples. Robert sent the poet’s <term>sirvente: a satirical poem used by troubadours to address political or personal grievances</term> against the Emperor to the King, his father; and in response, Charles restored the right that the poet had lost <note>This refers to the salt tax revenues on the Durance bridge mentioned on the previous page, which had been confiscated as punishment for Alamanon's earlier satires against the King.</note>. In this perilous career, one could be paid by some for the harm one said of others.

The *Rector of Arles* (Nostradamus <note>Jean de Nostredame, a 16th-century writer who wrote colorful, though often historically inaccurate, biographies of the troubadours.</note> should have said the Archbishop) also suffered a violent satire, which we shall describe. ## XXXV.

### HUGUES BRUNET.

This troubadour, born in Rodez, was destined for the clergy <note>original: "cléricature"</note> and received the education appropriate for that station. But what he gathered from his studies turned him away from the goal that had been set for him. The liveliness of his imagination was drawn only to the flowers of literature, and his natural aptitude inclined only toward those seductive subjects that inspired a taste for poetry. Instead of seeking his fortune through the paths of the ecclesiastical ministry, he sought it through those of the "agreeable talents" <term>talens agréables: A contemporary term for the performing arts, specifically the music and poetry of the medieval courts.</term>. He became a jongleur <term>jongleur: A wandering entertainer and minstrel who performed the works of troubadours, often traveling from court to court.</term>; he composed many pretty songs. The courts were opened to him. Alfonso, King of Aragon, the Count of Toulouse, the Count of Rodez, the Dauphin of Auvergne, and Bernard d’Anduse welcomed him in succession.

<summary>This page introduces the troubadour Hugues Brunet, describing his transition from a religious education in Rodez to a successful career as a poet and minstrel supported by various noble patrons.</summary>

Madame Galiana, a lady of the middle class <note>original: "bourgeoise"</note> from Aurillac, captured his heart, but without loving him in return. She loved the Count of Rodez; and if she seemed to encourage Brunet's passion, it was only so that she might be the subject of his poems.

The most remarkable praise the poet gives her is that she pleases everyone by speaking follies to fools, nonsense to the simple-minded <note>original: "sots"</note>, and witty things to the wise. For the rest, he constantly complains of her harshness. Ever since she told him one day with a laugh that nothing is obtained without boldness, he has not ceased to love her and to suffer.

> "What perplexity desolates me! I cannot escape the empire of love, which always promises me pleasures, and always overwhelms me with pains. This god lets himself be seen only through the imagination; he takes his sweet flight from the eye to the heart, from the heart into the mind; and he pierces me with his arrows <note>original: "traits"</note>. Conquered, subjugated by the beauty which he..."

The manuscript may therefore be at fault regarding the mistress of Brunet.

### XXXVI.

## FERRARI OF FERRARA.

We are translating from a manuscript in Modena the life of this troubadour, whom even Nostradamus <note>Jean de Nostredame (c. 1507–1577), a biographer of the troubadours whose accounts are often considered more legendary than historical</note> and Crescimbeni <note>Giovanni Mario Crescimbeni (1663–1728), an Italian critic and historian of poetry</note> did not know, and of whose works nothing remains. It contains interesting details.

Master Ferrari (as the historian calls him) was a *jongleur* <term>jongleur: a professional entertainer and musician who performed the poems of troubadours, often traveling between various noble courts</term> from Ferrara. No one in Lombardy <note>a region in Northern Italy where the Occitan language of the troubadours was highly prized in aristocratic circles</note> understood Provençal <note>the Occitan language used for lyric poetry in the Middle Ages</note> as well as he did, nor composed so well in that language: he produced very good and very beautiful books. He was a very courtly and God-fearing person. He willingly served knights and barons, and was constantly attached to the House of Este <note>one of the most powerful and long-lived noble dynasties in Italy, famous for their patronage of poets like Ariosto and Tasso</note>.

What follows is in a modern hand, in the margin of the manuscript.

## XXXVII.

### CADENET.

The castle of Cadenet on the Durance <note>A major river in southeastern France, historically significant as a boundary and trade route.</note>, in the county of Forcalquier <note>A historic region in Haute-Provence.</note>, belonged to a poor and unfortunate knight who was the father of our troubadour. The counts of Toulouse and Provence having allied themselves, in 1165, against William VI, Count of Forcalquier, this castle endured all the horrors of war; the people of Toulouse ruined it from top to bottom <note>original: "de fond en comble"</note> [1]. **CADENET** was still a child. A knight named William Hunaud of Lantur took him prisoner to Toulouse; but he had the generosity to act as a father to him; and the education he gave him would have produced better effects, if the young man, in forming his mind, had not attached himself to the frivolous rather than the useful <note>A common moralizing critique in 18th-century literary histories, suggesting that Cadenet preferred poetry and courtly pursuits over "useful" administrative or military skills.</note>.

Equipped with the imperial diploma <note>A formal legal document or decree issued by the Emperor, in this case Frederick I (Barbarossa), granting legal rights to the territory.</note>, Raymond Berenguer believed he needed assistance to strip the Count of Forcalquier of his lands. He turned to Raymond V, Count of Toulouse, and proposed they share the spoils. Their agreement was reached at Beaucaire, where they held a meeting in 1165. There, they concluded the marriage of the Count of Toulouse’s eldest son to Douce, the only daughter of the Count of Provence. Soon after, Raymond Berenguer entered the lands of the Count of Forcalquier. He was joined by his ally’s troops; it was then that the castle of Cadenet <note>A village and fortress in the Luberon region of Provence; it is the birthplace of the troubadour Cadenet.</note> suffered the disaster mentioned by our troubadour’s contemporary historian.

# XXXVIII.

## PERDIGON.

This troubadour is one of those who, from the most abject of conditions, rose to the highest heights through their talents; an example well-suited to encourage genius, but also capable of leading astray a crowd of mediocre minds, who are always eager to step outside their sphere to chase after fortune. Even talent rarely achieves such success without the help of intrigue.

PERDIGON was the son of a poor fisherman from L’Esperon, a town in the Gévaudan <note>A historical province in southern France, now primarily the department of Lozère.</note>. Born with wit and a pleasing appearance, he soon gave himself over to the ambition of finding access to the courts. He composed verses well, had a beautiful voice, played the violin <note>original: "violon"; in the context of the 12th century, this refers to the *vielle*, a bowed string instrument popular with troubadours.</note> perfectly, and lacked neither charm nor flexibility. He succeeded beyond his expec-

Finally, he conferred upon him the dignity of knighthood and made him his brother-in-arms; which was the height of favor.

Then Perdigon became a personage of importance in the region. He visited the barons and was welcomed everywhere with honor. The ladies competed for who should have him as a lover, or rather as the singer of their merit. His heart inclined only too much toward love. One sees from his pieces that he had a number of mistresses, and that they did not make him happy. Here is the best of his songs, in which he vividly expresses his sorrows.

## XXXIX.

### GUI or GUIGO.

We possess a number of pieces under the name of Gui, perhaps by the same troubadour <note>A medieval lyric poet and musician from southern France, composing in the Occitan language.</note>, or perhaps by several individuals whom it is impossible to distinguish, as no writer offers any clarity on this matter. It will therefore suffice to extract what may be interesting from these works. The author of the first pieces is named Gui or Guigo. ## GUI OR GUIGO.

**W**e have a number of pieces under the name of Gui, perhaps by the same troubadour, perhaps also by several whom it is impossible to distinguish, as no writer sheds light on this subject. In a satirical <term>sirvente</term> <note>A song of a political or satirical nature, often used to criticize public figures or social behavior.</note> against the same Bertrand:

He reproaches him for being stripped of all merit and all virtue, with a flabby body lacking both strength and worth.

### XL.

## BERENGER DE PALASOL.

Berenger de Palasol was, according to our manuscript biographies <note>original: "vies manuſcrites," referring to the *Vidas*, the short prose biographies of troubadours often included in medieval songbooks</note>, a Catalan knight from the county of Roussillon <note>A historic region in the eastern Pyrenees, now part of southern France</note>, poor, but distinguished by his appearance and his manners, joining the labors of knighthood with the pleasures of love and a taste for verse. Ermesine, wife of Arnaud d’Avignon and daughter of Marie de Pierrelatte, captivated his heart and became the subject of his songs. The historian of Languedoc <note>Likely a reference to the Benedictine authors of the *Histoire Générale de Languedoc*</note> counts him among the troubadours who flourished under Raymond V <note>Count of Toulouse from 1148 to 1194, and a noted patron of poets</note>, who died in 1194. We could establish this point of history through conjectures that are more than probable; but it would only result in tediousness without use.

It will be more useful to observe some errors by Nostradamus <note>Jean de Nostredame (1507–1577), the brother of the famous seer; he wrote biographies of the troubadours that are now known to be filled with historical fabrications and errors</note>. If he is to be believed—

<summary>This page introduces the troubadour Berenger de Palasol, a poor but noble Catalan knight known for his love songs dedicated to Ermesine of Avignon. The author situates him in the late 12th century and begins to critique the historical inaccuracies of Jean de Nostredame.</summary>

<keywords>Berenger de Palasol, Catalan troubadour, Roussillon, Ermesine, Raymond V, Jean de Nostredame, medieval biography</keywords>

Palafol was from Sisteron in Provence, the son of a physician attached to Queen Joanna <note>Joanna I (1326–1382), Queen of Naples and Countess of Provence. She had a tumultuous reign marked by the murders of her husbands and political intrigue</note>. Five magnificent tragedies, which he dedicated to Pope Clement VII <note>The first "Antipope" of the Great Western Schism, who resided in Avignon from 1378 to 1394</note>, earned him immortal glory. The first four had for their titles *Andrealla*, *Tarentala*, *Maillorquina*, *Allemanna*; allusions to the four husbands of Queen Joanna: Andrew of Hungary, Louis of Taranto, James of Majorca, and Otto of Brunswick. The last was entitled *Jehannella*, from the name of the princess. All five formed a portrait of her conduct, from childhood until her death. The author offered them secretly to the pope, from whom he received in reward a canonry <term>a ecclesiastical office or position within a cathedral</term> of Sisteron.

These bizarre works would have been quite suited to the prevailing taste. But dramatic art was always unknown to the troubadours. About four thousand pieces, which we have gathered from them, recall an infinity of the customs of their

The testimony of this historian <note>Referring to Jean de Nostredame, whose 16th-century biographies of troubadours are often considered more legendary than historically accurate.</note> is all the weaker here, as he is obviously mistaken regarding Blacas. He places his death in 1281; he attributes a song to him in which the Provençal people are blamed for having submitted to the House of Anjou, after having lived so happily under the House of Aragon; and from this he draws proof of the troubadour’s Aragonese origin. The work by Sordel <note>Sordello da Goito, a famous Italian troubadour. His funeral lament (planh) for Blacas is one of the most famous poems of the era.</note> concerning Blacas demonstrates that he had died several years before the marriage of Charles of Anjou to the heiress of Provence <note>Beatrice of Provence married Charles of Anjou in 1246. Since the lament for Blacas was written before this, the historian’s date of 1281 must be wrong.</note>.

### XLII.

# FOLQUET DE ROMANS.

All that our manuscripts teach us regarding this poet is that he was born in Romans, a town in the Viennois region <note>An ancient province in southeastern France, centered around the city of Vienne</note>; that he was a skilled <term>jongleur: a wandering entertainer who performed music and poetry</term> and was well-liked in the courts; that the nobility showered him with honors; and that he composed <term>sirventes: a genre of troubadour poetry, usually satirical or political, focusing on moral themes</term> to praise the virtuous and to rebuke the wicked. We learn from his own works that after having sung for some time in the Dauphiné <note>A historical province in southeastern France</note> of his love for a countess, he traveled to Italy, where he paid court to King Frederick, the Marquis of Montferrat, and particularly attached himself to the Lord of Carret, near Savona.

Frederick II, son of Emperor Henry VI, is certainly the king in question. In his childhood, he had received the investiture <term>investiture: the formal act of conferring a rank or office</term> of the Kingdom of Sicily; the Ita-

ly was for a long time his residence: he was elected emperor in 1212.

After the coronation of this prince, Folquet criticized him in a <term>sirvente: a type of satirical or political poem used by troubadours to address moral or social issues</term> in which he speaks out against the lack of generosity of his age.

> "I do not wish for my lord Frederick to enrich himself any further; for I hear it said by all those who come from his country, that he, who was seen to be so generous before becoming wealthy, now thinks of nothing but possessing lands and money."

The poet reminds him of this maxim: *By wanting to possess too much, one often loses everything.* He exhorts him to <term>liberality: the traditional noble virtue of being open-handed and generous with wealth</term>, for fear that if the wheel of fortune turned against him, he would become the laughingstock of his enemies. He blesses God who has given him a crown, and who has elevated his cousin the marquis. <note>This refers to William the Younger, Marquis of Montferrat, whose paternal grandmother was the sister of Emperor Conrad III, the great-grandfather of Frederick II.</note>

### LITERARY HISTORY

In another piece, he speaks of the same Lord of Montferrat, praising his virtues as superior to those of his father. <note>He refers to William VI, Marquis of Montferrat, whose father Boniface I was a leader of the Fourth Crusade and the first King of Thessalonica.</note> He says, however, that this lord greatly failed the Lombards by traveling to <term>Romania: a medieval term for the Byzantine Empire or the newly established Latin Empire in the East</term>; and he curses Thessaloniki, which for Lombardy has been the ruin of a great many people.

We have seen another <term>troubadour: a composer and performer of Old Occitan lyric poetry</term>, Elias Cairels, accuse the Marquis of Montferrat of a crime for delaying this expedition to Thessaloniki. This is how men are accustomed to judge: if war is not waged when they desire it, the princes are made out to be cowards; but if it has unhappy consequences, the princes were wrong to undertake it. The opinions of the common people vary constantly according to the whim of events.

We find new proof of this in two pieces by Folquet on the Crusade. Forgetting the calamities that these wars had produced, he strove to revive enthusiasm. He inveighs against—

> not come to us a prince powerful and wise enough
> to take the wealth from these
> wicked men, and bestow it upon anyone whose
> only title would be merit? Why
> are bad princes not changed, as
> abbots change their priors?"

There follows an exhortation to the good emperor, who has taken up the cross, to arm himself with courage in order to avenge the holy places. <note>The "good emperor" refers to Frederick II, whose long-delayed departure for the Holy Land was a frequent subject of troubadour poetry.</note>

The troubadour tasks his <term>sirvente: a song of satirical or political character</term> to cross Mount Cenis <note>A mountain pass in the Alps connecting France and Italy</note>, to tell the Lord of Carret <note>The del Carretto family were powerful lords in the Margraviate of Savona, Italy</note> that he should go to the land where our Savior was born, and that he should crown his entire glory with this expedition.

Folquet asks Tostemps; <note>Tostemps was another troubadour, though his identity is as debated as Folquet's.</note> Which he would prefer: to love a mistress who had no other lover but him, but who would not pretend to love him; or to love one who had for—

<header>LITERARY HISTORY, etc.</header>

Judging by such pieces, these famous battles of wit <note>The author refers here to the "tensons" or poetic debates common among the troubadours.</note> where the troubadours <note>Troubadours were the lyric poets and musicians of the 11th to 13th centuries who composed in the Occitan language of Southern France.</note> burned to distinguish themselves, produced nothing marvelous. A mediocre poet would succeed better today. But these weak attempts at art are useful to observe, if only to be convinced that ignorance long admired what has since been despised by taste and reason <note>The author reflects a typical 18th-century viewpoint, characterizing the medieval period as a time of "ignorance" compared to the "reason" of the Enlightenment.</note>.

### APPROVAL. <note>original: "Approbation." In the Ancien Régime of France, every book required official approval from a royal censor to ensure it contained nothing contrary to religion, the state, or public morals.</note>

I have read, by order of My Lord Chancellor, a Manuscript entitled: *Literary History of the Troubadours*, <note>The Troubadours were lyric poets and musicians of the 11th through 13th centuries, writing in Old Occitan. They are famous for their themes of courtly love and chivalry.</note> composed from the manuscripts of M. DE SAINTE-PALAYE. <note>Jean-Baptiste de La Curne de Sainte-Palaye (1697–1781) was a pioneering scholar of medieval French culture; he spent decades collecting materials that were later edited by others.</note> This Work is far superior to the *Lives of the Provençal Poets* by Nostradamus, <note>Jean de Nostredame (c. 1507–1577), the younger brother of the famous astrologer. His "Lives" were notorious among 18th-century scholars for being full of invented stories and historical inaccuracies.</note> which are filled with blunders & errors. The learned Academician and the skillful Editor * of his research seem to me to deserve, each for good reasons, the full favor of the Public. Done at Paris, this 27th of February, 1774.

->CAPPERONNIER,<-
->*Royal Censor.*<- <note>Jean Capperonnier (1716–1775) was a prominent classical scholar and the head of the King's Library.</note>

* M. l'Abbé MILLOT, of the Academies of Lyon & Nancy.

## THE KING’S PRIVILEGE. <note>original: "Privilége du Roi." This was a legal monopoly granted to a printer or bookseller, serving as an early form of copyright that also functioned as a final layer of state censorship.</note>

Louis, by the grace of God, King of France & Navarre: To our beloved and loyal Counselors, the People holding our Courts of Parliament & Superior Councils, Masters of Requests ordinary of our Household, the Provost of Paris, Bailiffs, Seneschals, their Civil Lieutenants, & our other Justices whom it may concern, GREETINGS. Our beloved Sieur DURAND the nephew, <note>Sieur Durand "neveu" refers to a member of the prominent Durand family of booksellers in Paris; adding "neveu" (nephew) distinguished his specific business branch.</note> Bookseller in Paris, has represented to Us that he desires to have printed and given to the Public, a Work entitled *The Literary History of the Troubadours*; should it please Us to grant him our Letters of Privilege necessary for this purpose. FOR THESE REASONS, wishing to treat [him] favorably...

<summary>This page features the official "Approbation" from the Royal Censor Capperonnier and the beginning of the "King's Privilege" (printing license) for the Literary History of the Troubadours. It highlights the scholarly transition from the unreliable 16th-century accounts of Nostradamus to the rigorous Enlightenment research of Sainte-Palaye and Abbé Millot.</summary>

the Petitioner, <note>original: "Exposant." This refers to the person requesting the license, in this case, likely the publisher or the author, Abbé Millot.</note> We have permitted & do permit him by these Presents, <note>original: "Présentes." A formal legal term referring to the document itself.</note> to have the said Work printed as many times as he shall see fit, & to sell it, cause it to be sold and distributed throughout our Kingdom, during the period of *six* consecutive years, counting from the day of the date of these Presents: We forbid all Printers, Booksellers & other persons, of whatever quality & condition they may be, from introducing any foreign printing [of this work] into any place under our authority: As also from printing or causing to be printed, selling, causing to be sold, distributing, or counterfeiting the said Work, nor to make any Extracts from it, under whatever pretext it may be, without the express and written permission of the said Petitioner, or those who shall have rights from him, <note>This refers to heirs or business partners to whom the publishing rights might be transferred.</note> under penalty of confiscation of the counterfeit Copies, and a fine of three thousand livres <note>The "livre" was the currency of France until 1795. Three thousand livres was a substantial sum, roughly equivalent to several years' wages for a skilled laborer.</note> against each of the Infringers, of which one third shall go to Us, one third to the Hôtel-Dieu of Paris, <note>The Hôtel-Dieu was the city's oldest and primary hospital; it was common practice in the Ancien Régime to direct a portion of legal fines to charitable institutions.</note> & the other third to the said Petitioner, or to the person who shall have rights from him, and of all costs, damages & interests; on the condition that these Presents shall be registered in full in the Register of the Guild of Printers & Booksellers of Paris, <note>original: "Communauté des Imprimeurs & Libraires." This was the professional corporation that regulated the book trade and enforced the King's privileges.</note> within three months of their date; that the printing of the said Work shall be done in our Kingdom & not elsewhere, on fine paper & with fine characters, <note>The Crown mandated high production standards (paper and typeface quality) to ensure the prestige of French book manufacturing.</note> that the Grantee <note>original: "Impétrant." The person who has obtained the legal grant or privilege.</note> shall comply in all things with the Regulations of the Book Trade, <note>original: "Réglemens de la Librairie."</note> & notably those of April 10, 1725, under penalty of forfeiture of the present Privilege; that before offering it for sale, the Manuscript which served as the copy for the printing of the said Work, shall be returned in the same state in which the Approval <note>The "Approbation" mentioned on the previous page, signed by the censor.</note> was given, into the hands of our very dear & loyal Kn[ight]... <note>The text cuts off here. It likely refers to the "Chevalier, Garde des Sceaux" (Knight, Keeper of the Seals) or the Chancellor, who oversaw the legal administration of the book trade.</note>
